author: Stanley
captionRaw:
90% of people scrolling on LinkedIn, think they have nothing to post about.
You’re wrong.
We all have:
→ Opinions
→ Individual perspectives
→ Lived experience and life learnings
If you’re still struggling…
Here are 9 types of posts you can write today:
(Broken down according to your goal)
GOAL: Grow your audience
1. The hot take
✅ Disagree with something your industry thinks is true
✅ Back it up with real experience or data
2. The problem reframe
✅ Take a problem your audience faces daily
✅ Describe it in a way they've never heard
3. The trend take
✅ Something is happening in your industry right now
✅ Share your specific opinion on it
GOAL: Building trust
4. The result
✅ A client went from X to Y (use real numbers)
✅ Show the before and the after
5. The framework
✅ A system or process you actually use
✅ Break it down step by step
6. The lead magnet
✅ Give something genuinely useful away for free
✅ A checklist, a template, a resource for their email in return
GOAL: Generating leads
7. The failure
✅ Talk about a time when you failed at something
✅ End with how you resolved it. One clear lesson
8. The objection
✅ What's stopping people from buying from you?
✅ Answer it before they ask
9. The demonstration
✅ Show your product solving a real problem
✅ Record a video or carousel to prove it
Next time you think you have nothing to say.
Come back to this list.

author: Elmer Lopez 🏆
captionRaw:
If I was starting my LinkedIn from 0 today, here’s exactly what I’m doing in the first 30 days:
Step 1: Optimize my Linkedin profile before I write a single post
When someone likes or comments on one of your posts, they’ll typically click on your profile within about 5 seconds.
So your profile needs to be optimized to answer: Who do you help? & how can you help me?
Step 2: Build a bank of 10 post ideas from conversations I already had
I'd go back through my last month of demos, discovery calls, and internal threads for content inspo.
Step 3: Comment on 10-20 posts a day from the exact people I want reading my content
Not "great post" comments.
Actual comments that add value on posts from the founders, buyers, and executives I want in my audience.
The algorithm starts showing you to their network, and their network is the one you're trying to reach.
1 strong comment alone could get you 5k impressions.
Now layer on the posting cadence.
3 posts/week for 30 days, even when a few flop here & there.
& here’s the thing, every single person who engages with your post is a warm lead you already have permission to talk to.
This is how to reach out to your content engagers:
1. Someone likes or comments
2. Check their profile to see if they're your ICP
3. Send the connection request
4. Once accepted, message them referencing the post they engaged with
Something like:
"Hey [Name], saw you commented on my post about [topic]. Curious if…..[insert pain you solve]
What would you add?

author: Jeremy Boissinot
captionRaw:
LinkedIn forcing me out of my paternity hibernation with this new feature, so obviously I had to react.
You'd think I'd love it, and I do applaud the anti AI-slop push LinkedIn has been running, but this specific button is counterintuitive.
Starting with the obvious one: people are terrible at spotting AI. What actually gets flagged is polished writing, non-native English speakers, and anyone with a clean structure. Meanwhile the actual slop farms sail through because they've learned to sound "human enough".
LinkedIn already claims their detection systems hit 94% accuracy. And I believe it, since I like to think we're able at Favikon to detect AI at a high level as well, even though we use patterns because posts only are not enough (AI-driven engagement is much easier to detect). But if your AI catches slop at 94%, you don't need my thumb. So this button is more a sentiment survey than anything else.
And the big one: you just handed every bot army and jealous competitor a free brigading weapon. Mass-report a creator as "AI slop" and let the algorithm do the dirty work. This already happens with regular reports, now it comes with a nice label. Fun fact: our page got removed after exactly this, a disgruntled creator with a low authenticity score asking his community to mass report our page as retaliation.
We've seen this movie before with the YouTube dislike button. It ended up telling you more about who the audience hated than about content quality, and YouTube eventually hid it for exactly that reason.
My take: this is marketing. LinkedIn wants to be seen fighting AI slop (they genuinely are, behind the scenes), but this button will change nothing except giving trolls a new toy. Which, ultimately, will have no effect because there's 0 chance LinkedIn would give that much power to people anyway.

author: Lara Acosta
captionRaw:
I spent the last 30 days breaking down how to build a $10k/mo content system on LinkedIn.
Here's the strategy you need that works (for any niche):
1. Find a profitable niche using this formula:
- Skill: What you are good at doing
- Market: The people who need it most and fast
- Problem: The painful problem your skill solves
- Value: The content you'll make based on the above
This is how you become undeniable on LinkedIn.
By getting clear on the exact problem you solve.
And how to talk about it in your content.
2. Write for all three audience tiers
- Diehards: Those who always engage with you
- Drive-bys: Those who've seen your content sometimes
- Drop-ins: Those who have 0 context on who you are
The key here is to optimize your content for the "drop-ins" - but most optimize for the "die hards".
A quick tip: Think about every post as a re-introduction.
Your hook should state either a result or proof you've done what you're about to educate them on.
Don't say: "How to grow your business"
Say: This system got 1,238+ new leads using email.
3. Build every post on the 5 P's
- Problem: name it better than your audience can
- Promise: show the transformation clearly
- Proof: back it with results and real stories
- Personality: let your tone do the selling
- Perspective: own the insight only you can give
4. Four lead-generation posts (that work every time)
- Celebrate a client win (for proof)
- Turn a framework into a lead magnet (for free leads)
- Show a before and after with real numbers (relatability)
- Use a story to then talk about your offer (story-selling)
Bonus tip: Collect transcripts from calls with leads, upload them to Kleo and let it write your next post based on specific pain points your ideal clients have.
Most people on LinkedIn are posting consistently.
But without a strategy to generate results.
And I'm tired of it, so I just shared my playbook with you.
Save this post for later, repost ♻️ it if it was useful!
P.S: Have you noticed when posts have a specific outcome, like a number or a timeline - the posts do better? Exactly what I'm saying!

author: Yonathan Levy
captionRaw:
You can build a LinkedIn carousel in 5 min in 2026.
The whole process runs in Claude Design, so the writing and the visuals happen in the same place instead of jumping between a doc and Canva.
1. Open Claude and go to Design.
2. Pick your design system, or create one by uploading your past carousels and brand assets so every slide comes out looking like yours.

4. Drop in one prompt telling Claude the topic and the carousel you want it to build.

Start with a cover slide, give every slide one clear point, and end on a strong CTA slide."

author: Stanley
captionRaw:
I analyzed 1,000 LinkedIn posts from January and June.
LinkedIn has changed (it always does).
But most of you are still playing by the old rules.
And wondering why you’re not growing.
Here’s the update you’ve all been waiting for:
Engagement:
❌ OLD: Comment anything because volume wins.
✅ NEW: Thoughtful comments drive reach. 15+ words.
→ Increased dwell time pushes your post.
Posting frequency:
❌ OLD: Post daily to stay visible.
✅ NEW: Posting 7x per week can kill reach.
→ Quality over quantity wins every time.
Post length
❌ OLD: Short, punchy, fast scrolls.
✅ NEW: Longer posts increase dwell time.
→ Posts that hold attention get distributed.
Hooks
❌ OLD: Hot takes and contrarian bait.
✅ NEW: Clear promise + credibility.
→ If you can’t back it up, people won’t read it.
Virality
❌ OLD: Go broad to go viral.
✅ NEW: Go narrow to grow.
→ Niche relevance beats mass appeal.
Links
❌ OLD: Links kill reach.
✅ NEW: Useless links kill reach.
→ Helpful links drive saves which increase reach.
Video
❌ OLD: Video for reach.
✅ NEW: Video for trust.
→ Videos help your audience get to know you.
Those crushing LinkedIn right now are focusing on:
- Depth over frequency
- Proof over performance
- Teaching over entertaining
Same LinkedIn.
New playbook.

author: Josh S.
captionRaw:
Your AI output is only as good as the prompt you're too lazy to write.
Blame the tool all you want... that won't fix the content.
I see people typing "make this better" into Claude
And wondering why the post flops.
The real issue is what you're typing into it.
Without specifics, Claude is just guessing too.
And then you get generic content that sounds like everyone else's AI slop on the feed.
Here are 12 swaps that'll change what you get back, starting today:
1. When you want to make something more professional:
❌ "Make it more professional"
✅ "Rewrite so my ICP, [describe them], finds it clear within 5 seconds"
2. When you want to improve the output:
❌ "Improve it"
✅ "Tighten it using 3 filters: clarity, rhythm, and one clear CTA"
3. When your post needs to be reduced:
❌ "Make it shorter"
✅ "Cut 30% without losing the core point or the hook"
4. When the post doesn't sound like you:
❌ "Make it sound natural"
✅ "Rewrite in the way I'd say it out loud, no LinkedIn jargon. Ask me if you need clarity on this"
5. When you want small fixes without changing your voice:
❌ "Fix this"
✅ "Fix the rhythm and spelling, leave the voice exactly as it is"
6. When you want the post to hit harder:
❌ "Make it more persuasive"
✅ "Rebuild around this objection my reader has: [objection]"
7. When you want options to choose from:
❌ "Give me 3 versions"
✅ "Give me 3 versions with different hook angles and tell me which one you'd publish and why"
8. When you're starting from a blank page:
❌ "Write me a LinkedIn post about X"
✅ "Write a LinkedIn post for a founder building [company] selling to [ICP], with a hook that names a specific pain in line one"
9. When you need a better hook format:
❌ "Make the hook better"
✅ "Give me 5 hook variations: One stat-led, one contrarian, one personal, one question-led, one story-led"
10. When you want a tailored carousel:
❌ "Write a carousel about X"
✅ "Write a 7-slide carousel: Slide 1 is the hook, slides 2-6 are one tactic each with an example, slide 7 is the CTA pushing to X"
11. When you need specific content ideas:
❌ "Give me content ideas"
✅ "Give me 10 post ideas a [founder type] would screenshot, based on this list of pain points: [paste pains]"
12. When you need a powerful CTA:
❌ "Write the CTA"
✅ "Write 3 CTA options: One for saves, one for comments, one for DMs. Tell me which fits this post best"
None of these are complicated.
They're just specific.
And specific is the entire difference between AI output that sounds like everyone else's and AI output that sounds like you.

author: Ruben Hassid
captionRaw:
Don't post (obvious) AI-written content.
Here are 12 tells to delete & the 11 skills that fix it:
(all 11 skills are free here → how-to-ai.guide)
Delete these from your writing today-
1. "Delve." You've never said it out loud. Once.
2. "Crucial/pivotal." Nothing is that pivotal.
3. "Tapestry." No human speaks like this.
4. "Here's the thing." There is no thing.
5. "Hope this helps." It doesn't. It outs you.
6. "After careful consideration." without considering
7. "to provide a quick update." Just give the update.
8. "Most people…" The lazy oversimplification.
9. "Robust / seamless / realm." The corporate AI.
10. Adverb abuse. "X quietly runs Y." Nothing runs.
11. "It's not X, it's Y." The famous AI sentence alive.
12. 'This isn't a budget. It's a statement of intent' No
Now my personally used 11 Claude skills that fix it:
1. /writer
Writes the first draft in your structure, not Claude's.
Good draft in = nothing to clean up later.
2. /editor
Cuts the fluff and the filler.
Every sentence earns its place or dies.
3. /fact-checker
Kills invented stats and fake-sounding quotes.
One hallucinated number and nobody trusts you again.
4. /anti-AI style
The base rewrite. Breaks the robotic rhythm
where every sentence is the same 18 words.
5. /ban-the-AI-words
Auto-blocks "delve," "crucial," "tapestry"
& the entire red list above.
6. /ban-the-AI-patterns
Kills "It's not X, it's Y" and the fake-deep endings.
The patterns out you faster than the words do.
7. /sound like your posts
Feed it 5 of your old posts. It writes like YOU, not like Claude. This one replaces every "humanizer" tool you've paid for.
8. /humanizer
Strips whatever AI smell is left.
Contractions in, em dashes out.
9. /red-pen
Flags your weak lines before your readers do.
10. /self-critique
Claude critiquing Claude beats Claude on the first try. It loops until the text reads clean.
11. /auto-block-banned-words
The safety net. Nothing on the red list ever ships again.
That's the whole setup.
12 tells deleted. 11 skills. 0 AI smell.

author: Andreas Horn
captionRaw:
The uncomfortable math of AI transformation: 10% is the model. 90% is work your organization hasn't budgeted for.
And that 90% is where almost every AI strategy quietly dies.
It almost always starts ambitious at the top: sized opportunities, an approved budget, transformation targets, the competitive-advantage language everyone nods at in the boardroom. Then it has to fall through the reality gap into the actual work. Siloed and poor data. Legacy systems that won't expose what you need. Compliance and risk. Change resistance. And the silent killer: no clear owner. The strategy doesn't fail loudly. It quietly stops being anyone's job.
This is the gap nobody budgets for, the distance between ambition and execution. The model was never the constraint. The operating model was.
What survives the fall has a spine the boardroom version skips: strategy, then operating model, then workflow redesign, then integration and data, then adoption and enablement, and only then business value. Each step is a handoff where strategy can die, and the two that get cut first are workflow redesign and ownership. Which is exactly why pilots inflate and nothing has moved six weeks later.
As far as I can tell, AI success is not a technology challenge. It is an execution problem, and the execution side does not improve on its own.
PS: Every week in Human in the Loop, I break down where AI actually creates value and where it just creates demos: https://lnkd.in/dbf74Y9E

author: Molly Stovold
captionRaw:
I grew my LinkedIn to 80k followers with only written content and the same repurposed photos.
And over two years that's made me more than half a millions dollars.
I've tried basically every way to monetise my personal brand.
Agency work. Brand deals. Digital products. Group cohorts. High-ticket 1:1s. Guest speaking.
Some of them made me really good money.
Many made me want to quit and go back to corporate where 9-5 honestly sounded easy in comparison.
Last year I ran a group cohort while seven months pregnant with my head in the loo every morning before the calls.
It nearly broke me.
Meanwhile, 1:1s paid well but took a lot of effort to deliver (rightly so, that is what you pay for).
And digital products sounded passive… launching them was far from it.
So now after all this trial and error I only do two things:
1. Run my Linkedin inbound marketing agency
2. Do brand partnerships.
That's it.
The agency gives me more than I ever made in coaching and I love love love the setup of having a team.
Brand deals pay me to talk about stuff I already use.
It took me three businesses and a lot of getting it wrong to figure out what actually works for how I want to live.
Not the most profitable setup on paper.
But the one that actually gives me the freedom I started building this personal brand for in the first place.

one person is doing all three jobs.

CFO: Cash. Financial strategy. Risk.
COO: Operations. Execution. Systems.
One founder. All three hats.

It means building a leadership team
and a structure that can run the company
without everything depending on you.
This is the stage where founders
have to stop being the entire C-suite
and start building one.
And this is exactly where many companies get stuck.
Because the company structure hasn't evolved
to meet the demands of growth.

drains you the most. That's your first hire.
2. Document the decisions only you can make.
Delegate everything else.
3. Build systems that let your team
operate without checking in with you daily.
The company can only grow as fast
as the leadership team beneath you.
Build the team. Define the roles.
Let go of the hats that aren't yours.

author: Ricky Waters’ post
captionRaw:
Don't get publicly shamed for your AI content.
These 10 tells are giving you away every time.
1. The Corporate Opener
↳ "In today's fast-paced world..." is the oldest AI first line alive.
2. Connector Overkill
↳ "Furthermore," "Moreover," "Additionally" signal AI instantly.
3. The Fence Sitter
↳ Presents both sides. Never takes a real stance. Real writers offend people or at least have conviction in what they say.
4. Predictable Sentence Rhythm
↳ Medium. Medium. Medium. Transition. Repeat.
5. Zero Personal Fingerprint
↳ No stories. No opinions. No mistakes. Could've been written by anyone, about anyone.
6. The Rule of Three Every Time
↳ Always three adjectives.
↳Always three examples.
↳Never seven.
(See what I did there?)
7. Telling Without Showing
↳ Claims "exceptional results." Never names the place, the person, or what actually happened.
8. Corporate Buzzwords
↳ "Delve," "leverage," "unlock." When did you last say "delve" out loud?
9. Hypothetical Examples Only
↳ "Imagine a founder who..." Never a real person. Never a real story.
10. Too Polished, Too Perfect
↳ No contractions. No fragments. No rough edges anywhere.
↳Spels evrything prfectly
You don't need all 10 to get caught.
You just need enough subtle clues to lose your reader.
Save this. Check it before every AI-assisted post.

🎯 The more specific you are the better
→ Niche down as fast as you can
→ Call out your target audience in the hook

2x MOFU: specific problems with real solutions

author: Roman Howe
captionRaw:
A few honest thoughts on AI written posts, from someone who works with Claude every day.
I as much as anyone am reading a lot of comments and articles over the last few months that do not sound anything like the person behind them. I would like to say the signs are small, but they too obvious.
People I admire, who I am fairly sure would never use an emoji, posting tons of them. Careful, factual people suddenly posting spicy takes that do not match how they actually talk.
I understand the pull, posting and commenting gets you reach, and handing the whole thing to AI is the quickest way to put out more.
I own it, I work with Claude on my own writing. And I have done some fairly heavy AI driven posts in the past. I want to say I've learned from it. Over time I built a setup that keeps my posts not only sounding like me, but actually mine.
Four things that make the difference for me:
1. I decide what I want to say and why before I start to work with Claude. A skill sets a minimum bar for input and makes Claude push back if I am taking a shortcut, so the thinking stays mine.
2. I built a skill that tells Claude how I write, in my own words, with real examples from things I wrote myself, emails, documents and so on. Worth making sure that what you give it as a basis is not itself AI generated.
3. I added a verification loop where a fresh agent reads the draft and flags anything that reads like AI, the generic lines, the inflated language, the phrasing I would never use.
4. I added a step where Claude asks me for my own view and pushes back when my answer is too generic. This keeps the post mine.
I really think sharing a real view, a personal thought, and reading other people's real views, is how we build common understanding, advance thinking, and have real discourse.

author: Magali De Reu
captionRaw:
A year ago, my founder client got 0 replies to his DMs. Yesterday he closed $25K in one thread. The ONE thing he changed? He stopped selling:
This guy knows how to sell. He's closed deals for years, just not on LinkedIn. Sound familiar?
Your sales skills are fine. Your DMs just stink of need. I've seen pressure leak in ways you don't notice:
- your questions give them nothing to grab onto
- your follow-ups sound fine to you but not to them
- you're asking for more than they're ready to give
You don't feel pushy, but your DMs do. My flow flips that at all 3 points:
1/ Hand them an easy exit
After your first DM, ask a 3-option question. Straight from my inbox:
"Thanks for connecting! Saw your post about your exit, sounds exciting. Curious, are you building a new venture, keeping your visibility up, or just letting it all soak in for now?"
Two real options, plus a third that lets them walk away clean. People reply when they don't feel trapped.
2/ Affirm the identity you share
Close with affinity. Hint you're in for the long game.
"Always love connecting with fellow founders who are this ready for what's next."
3/ Lower the risk
Once the need is on the table, match it with one tiny step. "Want me to show you how I did this for a founder in your spot?"
All it takes is one yes, with no leap attached.
And if they go quiet? So f*cking be it. Life happens. Follow up 3x max in a week, then move on.
My client got ignored 5 times before the $25K landed. I close 88% of my leads the same way.
Stop selling and they'll start buying. 🤘
PS: I'm running a €1 workshop next week on the 3 posts that got me €28K from warm leads in June. Click 'visit my website' to get in.

author: Angad S.
captionRaw:
The legends of Lean disagreed on almost everything but one...
"A good person cannot outwork a broken process."
Each of them stared at the same problem you face every day. Things go wrong on the floor. Defects, delays, mistakes that should not have been possible. And every one of them refused the easiest answer in the room, the one that points a finger at whoever was standing closest to the failure. They looked straight past the operator and went after the system instead.
Look at what each one actually did:
1. Toyoda gave the machine the power to stop itself, so no tired human had to catch every fault.
2. Ohno walked to the problem instead of summoning it to a meeting.
3. Shingo designed the mistake out of the process instead of scolding it out of the person.
4. Deming put the system on trial and let the operator go free.
5. Ishikawa handed the problem to the people closest to it, not the people above it.
6. Imai made improvement small enough that everyone could do it, every day.
Now notice what is missing from that list. Not one of them built a tool to make people care more, try harder, or finally pay attention. They assumed their people were already capable. Then they built systems worthy of them.
A century of the sharpest minds in manufacturing kept reaching the same verdict. They were not being soft on the worker. They had simply learned what Deming said plainly: a bad system will beat a good person every time. And they were done losing to one.

LinkedIn's profile now impacts your post ranking.

When someone saves your post, they're bookmarking it to use later.

Consistency matters more than volume while posting on LinkedIn.

Start tracking these metrics.

author: Eric Partaker
captionRaw:
I used to pride myself on being busy.
Back-to-back meetings.
Overflowing inbox.
Working late.
Until my mentor asked me one question that changed everything:
"Are you actually getting anything done?" That hit hard.
I was busy, but I wasn't productive.
I was working on everything, but accomplishing nothing important.
That's when I learned the secret: the best leaders don't work harder. They guard their time, focus on high-impact work, and eliminate nearly everything else
12 proven techniques to master your time like a Fortune 500 CEO:
1. Eisenhower Matrix
↳ For when you’re busy but not productive
↳ Separate urgent from important (and don’t confuse the two)
2. SMART Goals
↳ Big dreams mean nothing without a plan
↳ Get specific, set a deadline, and track progress
3. Timeboxing
↳ Multitasking kills focus
↳ Block time for deep work, and watch your productivity skyrocket
4. ABCDE Method
↳ If everything is a priority, nothing is
↳ Rank tasks A to E, and never waste time on the bottom
5. Pomodoro Technique
↳ For when you lose steam at midday
↳ Work in focused 25-minute sprints with breaks to stay sharp
6. Kanban Board
↳ For when you feel overwhelmed
↳ A simple "To-Do, In Progress, Done" board clears mental clutter fast
7. Eat the Frog
↳ If you’re procrastinating that tough task
↳ Do it first. The rest of your day will feel effortless
8. 1-3-5 Rule
↳ Stop overloading your to-do list
↳ Win the day: 1 big task, 3 medium, 5 small
9. MoSCoW Method
↳ Not sure where to focus?
↳ Label tasks as Must, Should, Could, or Won't to cut the clutter
10. 168 Hours Time Tracking
↳ Think you're always running out of time?
↳ Track a full week. You'll find gaps you never knew existed.
11. Warren Buffett's 5/25 Rule
↳ Success doesn’t come from doing more
↳ List 25 goals, focus on 5, ignore the rest completely
12. Getting Things Done (GTD)
↳ Too many ideas but not enough action?
↳ Capture everything, organize by priority, and execute systematically.
You can't scale your impact if you're drowning in busywork.
Small shifts in how you spend your hours create massive changes in your results.
The bad news is time flies. The good news is, you're the pilot.

captionRaw:
Most people are using beginner AI tools and wondering why experts outpace them.
The gap isn't intelligence.
It's not even effort.
It's the tools they reach for.

ChatGPT for everything.

author: Sarah Hurzeler
captionRaw:
One of the fastest ways to slow down an organization:
Ask managers, directors, and VPs to do the same job.
A manager, director, and VP may all lead teams…
But they are not interchangeable roles.
→ Managers run today
→ Directors build how work runs
→ VPs decide where the business goes
The strongest organizations understand this:
Each leadership level creates a different type of leverage.
- Managers drive execution.
- Directors connect strategy to scalable operations.
- VPs align teams, resources, and priorities to business outcomes.
When those levels blur, problems show up fast:
- Directors buried in tactical firefighting
- VPs pulled into daily decisions
- Managers expected to solve strategic gaps without authority
That’s usually when:
Speed slows
Accountability blurs
Teams become reactive instead of aligned
One thing I’ve learned over the years in operations & supply chain:
High-performing organizations need all three levels operating well simultaneously.
Every level matters.
Every role matters.
Great companies don’t succeed because of one strong executive or one strong operator. They succeed when leadership layers are aligned and each role is empowered to do the work it was designed to do.

author: Eric Partaker
captionRaw:
The Japanese secret that makes success feel effortless.
You don't need big breakthroughs. You need Kaizen.
It's a Japanese idea. It means "change for the better." Small steps, repeated, that add up to big change over time.
I know it works because I lived it. After a health scare, I didn't flip a switch. I changed one small thing at a time.
Most of my coaching clients think they don't have time for small steps. They've just gotten used to a lower baseline and called it normal.
Why Kaizen works:
✅ It's simple and easy to keep up
✅ It builds momentum fast
✅ It turns mistakes into fuel
How to put it to work:
1. Pick one thing. Ask what one change would matter most.
2. Learn from mistakes, then move on.
3. Stack small wins. Prove every day you're becoming who you want to be.
4. Listen to feedback. People see what you can't.
5. Stay consistent. Make it part of your daily routine.
6. Bring others in. Kaizen loves company.
7. Reflect, then set new goals.
8. Keep it simple. The best changes usually are.
9. Be patient. Good things take time.
10. Never stop. There's always a better way.
Start small. Stay steady. One day you'll look back and see how far you've come.

author: Colleen Paulson
captionRaw:
I was invited to participate in LinkedIn's Mastermind program last year. In the past year of using these principles, I generated 13M impressions.
Here are 3 takeaways that anyone can use:
1. Focus on one nugget per post: Narrow in one key takeaway that you are giving your audience. In my post that performed that best, I focused on one key data point (vs the 4 data points that I might have typically shared).
2. Add your take to a current news story: For example, Procter & Gamble announced that it was laying off 7,000 employees last year. I started my career at P&G, so I wrote a post giving my insider take on the news and what this might mean for the market as a whole. It was picked up by LinkedIn News and generated some great discussion.
3. Make your subject clear in the first 2 lines of your post: I've been expanding my hooks to tell more of the post story and provide context to draw the reader in.
Bonus tip: "Broetry" is out. LinkedIn emphasized that inserting extra blank lines (formerly known as "broetry") isn't the best way to write here. Write in paragraphs as you normally would.
There's a lot more, but with the one nugget per post strategy, I'll stop here. Thanks to the LinkedIn team for the invite and for sharing powerful, practical strategies that anyone can use to better help their audience.

author: Eric Partaker
captionRaw:
85% of leaders regretted a major decision last year.
I've coached 650+ CEOs.
Every one of them has been there.
And I have too, of course.
The decision that keeps you up at 2am.
The one you overthought until the window closed.
The one you rushed when you should have slowed down.
The gap between a good call and a costly one is preparation.
The best CEOs pick their decision tool before the pressure hits.
7 decision frameworks worth keeping close:
1/ The Eisenhower Matrix
→ Sort by urgency and importance
→ Do it, schedule it, delegate it, or delete it
2/ The OODA Loop
→ Observe, Orient, Decide, Act
→ Built for fighter pilots. Works for fast markets.
3/ One-Way vs. Two-Way Doors
→ Reversible? Move fast.
→ Irreversible? Slow down.
4/ The ICE Method
→ Score options by Impact, Confidence, and Ease
→ Pick the highest score. Stop debating.
5/ The SPADE Framework
→ One person decides. Everyone else is heard.
→ Kills the "who's actually in charge" problem.
6/ The Premortem
→ Assume the decision already failed
→ Work backward. Fix it before you commit.
7/ The 10/10/10 Rule
→ How will you feel in 10 minutes, 10 months, 10 years?
→ Strips the emotion out of the decision.
That last one is the one I lean on most.
10 minutes in, you're scared.
10 months later, you're glad you did it.
10 years later, you've made that call 20 times.
You're bulletproof.
What's your go-to framework for tough decisions?

author: Eric Partaker
captionRaw:
90% of companies stall before they’re able to scale.
Not because the market changed.
Not because the team isn’t capable.
And certainly not because they lack vision.
They stall because their operations can’t keep up with their growth.
I’ve seen it over and over.
The CEO is still making too many decisions.
Processes live in people’s heads.
Everyone’s working hard, but execution is inconsistent.
So the team starts spinning.
Firefighting replaces focus.
And big goals turn into reactive checklists.
When that happens, the fix isn’t more hustle.
It’s operational discipline.

Operational excellence isn’t one big change.
It’s a layered process. Built step by step.
You start with standardization.
Create one clear way to do the work. No more “everyone has their own method.”
Then you move to automation.
Eliminate repetitive tasks. Free up time for deeper work.
Next comes measurement.
Track the right numbers. Make them visible. Let the data guide your decisions.
Then, layer in continuous improvement.
Small weekly fixes. Fast iterations. Constant learning.
Only then are you ready for real innovation.
Not chaos disguised as creativity. Bold ideas that stick, scale, and move the business forward.
This isn’t a theory.
It’s how strong, sustainable companies actually scale.
From startups to 8-figure teams, the pattern is the same.
Build the layers in order.
Tighten the engine before you step on the gas.
Save this for when growth gets messy.

author: Josh S.
captionRaw:
90% of a viral LinkedIn post depends on 1 thing.
Get it wrong, and the whole post could flop...
The hook determines whether people engage with your post or move on.
I've written hooks across 100s of accounts.
After 1,000+ posts tested across multiple brands,
The formats winning 12 months ago aren't getting reach anymore.
In 2024, curiosity hooks dominated.
They were vague and clickbait-adjacent.
"You won't believe what happened next" energy.
In 2026, authority hooks win.
And the algorithm prioritises content that gets read by the right people.
Your hook needs to do 2 things at once:
Stop the scroll, and signal who the post is for.
Here's the complete hook writing playbook for 2026:
1️⃣ How To
Lead with a powerful statement and drop the "how to" on line 2.
↳ Best for: Top of funnel reach and saves.
↳ Example: Delegation is the most underrated leadership skill. Here's how to do it properly:
2️⃣ How I
Lead with a specific result and a timeframe.
↳ Best for: Trust building and conversion content.
↳ Example: How I generated 23,000 leads in 30 days. Without running a single ad:
3️⃣ Contrarian
Make a strong, polarising claim.
↳ Best for: Reach, comments, and challenging bad advice.
↳ Example: Most LinkedIn advice is making your content worse. Here's what to do instead:
4️⃣ Shocking Stats
Lead with a number that stops the reader cold.
↳ Best for: Awareness content and broad reach.
↳ Example: 95% of LinkedIn posts get fewer than 1,000 impressions. Here's why yours is one of them:
5️⃣ Open Promise
Make a bold promise based on a credible result. Add a timeframe.
↳ Best for: Mid and bottom of funnel content.
↳ Example: This one change grew a LinkedIn account by 400% in 3 months. Here's exactly what changed:
Hook formats evolve, but the formatting rules never do:
Line 1: 62 characters maximum.
Line 2: 50 characters maximum.
No bold or italics in the hook, ever.
1 clear idea per hook.
Authority, specificity, and ICP relevance are doing more work in 2026 than shock alone.
Ask yourself this after every hook you write:
Would this stop me from scrolling?
If the answer isn't an immediate yes, rewrite it.
Hooks are the highest leverage skill on LinkedIn right now.
1 line can double your reach, or kill it entirely.
Start treating them like they matter that much.
What's a hook that made you stop scrolling recently?

author: Nader Alnajjar
captionRaw:
The secret behind the top 1% of LinkedIn creators:
Their content includes these 9 types of posts 👇
I've spoken to founders with 100k followers who haven't closed a deal from LinkedIn in months.
And founders with 2k followers who are turning away work.
Post format is a big part of that.
A personal story does something a listicle can't.
A case study does something a thought leadership post can't.
They're not interchangeable.
To have a successful content strategy where you get attention, build trust with your audience AND get them to convert...
You need a mixture of these 9 types of LinkedIn posts:
(Scroll through the slides to see real examples of each + extra insights)
1️⃣ Thought Leadership
↳ Take a clear stance on something in your industry
↳ This is what gets you known FOR something, not just known
2️⃣ Personal Story
↳ Share an authentic moment that builds trust and makes you memorable
↳ People buy from people they feel they know. A story does that faster than any credential
3️⃣ Cheat Sheet
↳ Break down a framework in a way people want to save (saves are one of the highest-value signals on LinkedIn)
↳ The best cheat sheets solve a problem someone has right now, in clear actionable steps
4️⃣ Infographic
↳ Make a complex idea easy to understand at a glance, with visuals to help
↳ These travel well. People share visuals far more than they share text posts
5️⃣ Carousel
↳ Walk people through a process in a way that keeps them swiping (good for dwell time)
↳ These work best if you want to explain something in a more story-led way
6️⃣ Listicle
↳ Deliver quick, scannable value people can act on immediately
↳ Low barrier to read, high likelihood to share. One of the easiest formats to get traction with
7️⃣ Case Study
↳ Show a real result/transformation, the strongest trust-builder you have
↳ A good case study answers the question a prospect has before they even ask it
8️⃣ Impression Post
↳ These introduce you to people who've never come across your more specific content
↳ The caption is where you add your angle so it's not just generic, motivational slop
9️⃣ Resource Curation
↳ Round up the best tools, resources or reads in your space
↳ Saves and follows are extremely high on these because people want to come back to the list
If your content is getting reach but no leads, you're probably heavy on one end of this list.
If it's getting neither, you might be missing the formats that pull people in first.

author: Sarah Hurzeler
captionRaw:
Forecasts don’t buy inventory.
Plans don’t place POs.
Buyers do.
And this is where many inventory problems quietly begin.
Most organizations talk about forecasting and planning.
Far fewer talk about the connection between forecasting, planning, and buying.
But all three drive inventory performance together.
→ Forecasting: Builds the demand signal using history, trends, and market inputs.
→ Planning: Translates that signal into inventory, capacity, and supply decisions.
→ Buying: Turns those decisions into real cash commitments and inventory receipts.
The relationship that matters:
Forecasting predicts demand.
Planning positions supply.
Buying commits cash.
Where organizations struggle is in the gap between the three.
- The forecast shifts.
- The plan lags.
- The buy order is already placed.
That’s when problems compound:
- Inventory building ahead of demand
- Short buys on fast-moving SKUs
- Excess working capital exposure
- Margin pressure from reactionary purchasing
- Service levels slipping during volatility
Strong operators understand:
- Forecasting improves visibility.
- Planning improves readiness.
- Buying determines financial exposure.
The real challenge is not optimizing one function independently.
It’s aligning all three fast enough to respond to changing demand.
Question for Operators: Where does your organization see the biggest disconnect today...forecasting, planning, or buying?

author: Will McTighe
captionRaw:
LinkedIn isn't too crowded.
Starting from zero in 2026 is actually the easiest it's been in years.
When Chris and I analyzed 397K posts earlier this month, we found the gap between the top 1% and the average creator is shrinking.
When I started in 2024, a big audience was a massive advantage. Big accounts got more early engagement.
But that advantage is gone. Follower count is not what wins on LinkedIn.
So if I were starting in 2026, this is the exact system I'd follow:
1/ How to go viral
Virality = topic + first line + visual. All 3 need to stop the scroll before someone clicks "see more."
Pick a topic your audience is already interested in. Make line 1 a specific promise, problem, or surprise (authority, personal story, or humor), and pair it with a visual interesting enough to stop the scroll.
2/ Set a content strategy
LinkedIn posts do 1 of 3 things: grow your audience, build trust, or drive sales. Most people stick to growth content cuz it's easier, but growth alone won't convert anyone into a lead.
Post educational infographics and carousels 4x a week to grow, personal stories 2x a week to build trust, and case studies 1x a week to drive leads.
3/ Write for LinkedIn
The best posts are between 1,250 and 3,000 characters. That gives you enough space to set up the problem, make people care, and give them something useful.
Make sure your posts read like you speak. No one wants to read a formal report or a try-hard joke.
4/ Post more videos
Video builds trust better than almost any other format.
Use it for educational content, stories and skits, or client testimonials. One video a week is enough.
5/ Create lead magnets
Build a freebie that solves one narrow, painful problem for your target audience. A prompt library, a checklist, a template, or a swipe file all work.
Give it away in exchange for an email.
6/ LinkedIn power hour
You don't need to spend all day on LinkedIn. All you need is a daily system - I recommend the power hour.
Comment thoughtfully on 5-10 posts in your niche. Share a post that solves a real problem for your audience. Reply to every comment you get within the first hour. Then DM the people who engaged with you.
Anyone can start building a personal brand today. Don’t fall behind.

author: Safa Abdulhadi Alshafai
captionRaw:
Here is a highly concise, executive summary of the Supply Chain Metrics cheat sheet. It condenses the 14 key performance indicators into 4 core operational pillars for fast, high-level review.
1. Demand & Capacity Planning
Forecast Accuracy: Measures variance between forecasted and actual demand to reduce planning variability.
Capacity Utilization: Tracks actual vs. maximum possible production output to balance underutilization against operational overload.
2. Sourcing, Inventory & Cost Efficiency
Inventory Turnover & Days of Inventory (DOI): Dual metrics tracking asset efficiency—how fast stock sells versus how many days of supply are tied up in inventory.
Total Landing Cost: Captures the true, fully burdened cost of an item (Price + Freight + Duties + Handling).
Cash-to-Cash Cycle Time: Measures total days cash is frozen between paying suppliers (DPO) and collecting revenue (DSO), influenced by inventory velocity (DIO).
3. Warehouse & Logistics Speed
Dock-to-Stock Cycle Time: Measures the internal throughput speed from receiving goods to warehouse stock availability.
Order-to-Delivery Lead Time: Tracks total elapsed time from the initial customer order date to the final physical delivery date.
Supply Chain Cycle Time: An end-to-end macro metric covering the entire SCOR model workflow: $\text{Plan} \rightarrow \text{Source} \rightarrow \text{Make} \rightarrow \text{Deliver} \rightarrow \text{Return}$.
4. Customer Fulfillment & Service Level
Perfect Order Rate: The ultimate reliability standard—orders delivered on time, complete, damage-free, and accurately documented.
On-Time In-Full (OTIF): Measures the baseline execution performance of delivery punctuality and completeness.
Fill Rate vs. Backorder Rate: Inverse indicators tracking immediate product availability from stock versus the percentage of demand delayed due to stockouts.

author: Marek Dabrowski
captionRaw:
Most plants don’t have a Lean problem.
They have a layer problem.
They try to improve culture before standard work exists.
They ask for accountability before the work is visible.
They install dashboards before people agree what “normal” looks like.
They run Kaizen events before daily management is stable.
And then everyone wonders why the improvement doesn’t hold.
A Lean operation is built in layers:
1. Standard work
2. isual management
3. Daily management
4. CI systems
5. Culture
Culture is NOT where you start.
Culture is what shows up after the lower layers become real on the floor.
If the standard is unclear, the board won’t save you.
If the board is ignored, the meeting won’t save you.
If the meeting has no action, the culture won’t change.
Start where the work happens.
Make the standard VISIBLE.
Then manage the gap every day.
That’s where Lean starts to hold.

author: Roopam Jain
captionRaw:
Everyone talks about ML in supply chain. Almost nobody talks about which model, for which decision, and why.
After 18+ years across ecommerce, global supply chain & logistics, and PE consulting - here's what actually works in production, and when:
1. Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM) → Demand Forecasting
Best when relationships are non-linear and error costs are asymmetric. Stockout and overstock are not equal business problems - your model needs to know that. This approach consistently delivered 5–10% YoY unit cost reductions across complex, multi-node fulfillment networks.
2. Random Forest → Fraud & Anomaly Detection
Returns fraud is adversarial and constantly evolving. Random Forest’s ensemble approach handles that variance beautifully. The underrated benefit here is explainability. In high-stakes operations, showing why a transaction was flagged matters as much as accuracy.
3. Logistic Regression → CX and operational Escalation Triggers
When building agentic AI for live operations and customer experience flows, this is the ideal escalation model to decide when to hand off from bot to human. It offers calibrated probability output, speed, and total interpretability. When a wrong call costs you a customer, interpretability becomes a governance requirement.
4. K-Means Clustering → Portfolio Classification
When advising PE funds, using K-Means on target portfolios surfaces hidden groupings-similar cost structures, revenue trajectories, or risk profiles-that are invisible to traditional financial models. Companies that look identical on a DCF often separate into entirely different risk clusters. Unsupervised learning shows you the structure human intuition misses.
The ultimate lesson? Model selection is a product and business decision, not just a data science decision.
Start with the operational decision you need to make better. The model follows.
What are you seeing in your organization - are teams picking models for the right reasons, or just chasing the latest hype cycle?

author: Kaleab Shimels’ post
captionRaw:
"Our on-time delivery rate is 97%."
Sounds great. But, 97% of what?
Line items shipped? Orders fully complete? Value delivered? On time by whose clock, yours or the customer's?
The metric you choose changes the story entirely. Here are 3 supply chain KPIs I've been learning about that are easy to track wrong:
1. On-Time In-Full (OTIF)
Most teams track "on-time" OR "in-full" separately. OTIF combines both, an order is only a win if it arrives complete AND on schedule. Tracking them apart hides the real fill rate problem.
2. Inventory Turnover
A high turnover ratio looks healthy. But if you're turning inventory fast because you're constantly running lean and expediting orders, that's a cost problem disguised as a performance win.
3. Supplier Lead Time
Averages are misleading here. A supplier with an average 10-day lead time might swing between 4 and 18 days. The variance matters more than the mean, and most dashboards don't show it.
I'm still learning the nuances of all three, so I'd love to be challenged on this.

Variability
↳ Immature: assumes a stable plan and reacts when it breaks

Forecast
↳ Immature: single numbers, example: “Forecast = 100K”
↳ Mature: ranges, example: “Forecast = 90–110K, here’s how we respond”
Constraints
↳ Immature: discovers bottlenecks when service drops
↳ Mature: knows what will break before it does
Trade-offs
↳ Immature: avoids difficult choices
↳ Mature: makes trade-offs visible; service vs inventory; cost vs responsiveness
Reaction to Noise
↳ Immature: adjusts plans constantly
↳ Mature: separates signal from noise and protects plan stability
Decisions
↳ Immature: waits for more data
↳ Mature: makes informed decisions with imperfect data
Alignment Before the Meeting

author: Yonathan Levy
captionRaw:
LinkedIn replaced its algorithm with a single AI system.
And it works differently from what you are used to.
Every post now goes through four stages before it reaches anyone.
Quality check, testing, distribution, and matching.
1. The first stage filters out spam and engagement bait instantly.
2. The second stage shows your post to a small group and watches what happens. If people engage, distribution expands and if they scroll past, it stops.
3. Who sees it after that depends on how often they interact with you and how closely your topic matches their activity.
4. The algorithm then matches your post to users based on topic, language, and mentioned companies.
A few numbers worth knowing:
Comments now carry 15x more weight than likes.
One save drives 5x more reach than a like and 2x more than a comment.
Posts with 60+ seconds of dwell time hit 15.6% engagement.
Posts with under 3 seconds hit 1.2%.
Once you see how it works, you post differently.

author: Hashim H.
captionRaw:
S&OP Explained: Aligning Demand, Supply, and Business Goals!
Many companies struggle not because they lack demand.
They struggle because sales, operations, finance, and supply chain are not aligned.
This is where S&OP becomes powerful.
S&OP stands for Sales and Operations Planning.
It is a structured business planning process that connects:
✔ Demand planning
✔ Supply planning
✔ Inventory planning
✔ Production capacity
✔ Financial targets
✔ Customer service goals
The main purpose of S&OP is simple:
Create one agreed business plan across all departments.
Without S&OP, companies often face:
• Forecast errors
• Excess inventory
• Stock shortages
• Production delays
• Poor communication
• Conflicting department priorities
A strong S&OP process usually includes:
Demand review
Supply review
Gap analysis
Financial alignment
Executive decision-making
Continuous performance tracking
Example:
Sales may forecast higher demand for a product.
But supply chain must check:
• Do we have enough inventory?
• Can suppliers support the volume?
• Is production capacity available?
• What is the financial impact?
S&OP helps companies move from reactive firefighting to proactive planning.
In supply chain, alignment is just as important as accuracy.
What do you think is the biggest challenge in S&OP — forecasting, communication, or execution?

author: Carol Ptak
captionRaw:
A CEO told me last month that his supply chain team is running flat out and falling further behind every quarter.
I asked him what tools they were using. MRP. Forecast-driven. Same system they installed in 1998 getting ready for the Y2K crisis.
I asked him what had changed since 1998.
He laughed.
EVERYTHING.
Customer expectations.
Product complexity.
Lead time pressure.
Supplier reliability.
Demand volatility.
Geopolitics.
The only thing that didn't change is now it is a real crisis.
Everything changed. The planning tools did not.
MRP was designed in the 1960s for a stable world with predictable demand and reliable supply. That world is gone. It has been gone for a long time. And the planning profession has been absorbing the consequences every single day.
Your planners are not failing. Their tools are failing them.
I know because I have been on that shop floor. I started at minimum wage. I have run the plant. I have sweated payroll. And I have stared at a screen full of exception messages knowing that the system is telling me to do things that will make the problem worse.
The answer is not a better forecast. The answer is not a fancier algorithm. The answer is not AI layered on top of broken logic.
The answer is to stop pushing product based on predictions and start pulling based on what is actually happening. Successful companies sense and adapt to the world around them. Agility with stability. But how?
Strategically placed decoupling points. Buffers that adjust dynamically. Execution visibility your planners can trust without building a shadow system in Excel.
Roughly right is better than precisely wrong.
The methodology exists. It works in pharma, automotive, chemicals, consumer goods, aerospace. Across six continents. In companies with 50 employees and companies with 50,000.
The only barrier is the deep belief that "this is just how supply chain is."
It is not. I have spent 50 years proving it is not.
What planning assumption is your company still running on that everybody knows is wrong but nobody will say out loud?

✅ Historical trends
✅ Promotions & pricing
✅ Market intelligence
✅ POS / downstream signals

✅ AI-assisted forecasting

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
⚙️ LAYER 2 — SUPPLY PLANNING
“How will the network respond?”
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Depending on the business model, this may involve:
🏭 Manufacturing planning
📦 Inventory planning
🚚 Replenishment planning

This is where most supply chain trade-offs are made.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

How to land roles you're not qualified for: job descriptions are wishlists not requirements. If you meet sixty to eighty percent of qualifications apply anyway. USC Career Center research shows employers want people willing to learn and take challenges not perfect matches.
Strategy one transferable skills: show what you can do not what you've done. Examples project management, communication, problem-solving, leadership. Frame it: instead of I've never done X say I developed similar skills doing Y here's how it transfers. Research shows employers teach technical skills can't teach reliability initiative adaptability.
Strategy two quantify accomplishments: results beat experience. Wrong approach managed social media. Right approach grew Instagram from five hundred to fifteen thousand in six months resulting in forty percent increase website traffic. Formula action plus context plus measurable result equals proof of capability.
Strategy three network your way in: CareerShifters research networking avoids ruthless CV filtering. Request informational interviews twenty-minute coffee chats, ask about their path role company culture, show enthusiasm willingness to learn. Many jobs filled through referrals before posted.
Strategy four tailor every application: 2025 data ninety-seven percent Fortune 500 use ATS with AI filters. Identify five to ten repeated terms in job description, naturally include in CV, use standard fonts, avoid graphics. Beat ATS speak their language.
Strategy five address gaps directly: acknowledge then pivot to strengths. Script I don't have X years but here's what I do have that's relevant. Showcase related experience, quick learning ability, passion, plan for closing gaps through courses certifications.
Strategy six demonstrate willingness to learn: growth mindset beats experience. Mention courses taken, share examples learning quickly past roles, ask questions about development opportunities, express excitement about growth. Companies want people who close gaps fast.
Strategy seven create proof of work: when lack formal experience create own evidence. Marketing create sample campaigns, design build portfolio spec work, analyst analyse public datasets share findings LinkedIn. You've proven capability no longer unqualified.

author: Marcia D Williams’ post
captionRaw:
Bad metrics set demand and supply planners up for failure.
This infographic shows 10 metrics demand & supply planners CANNOT ignore:
Demand Planner
# 1. MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error)
↳ Measures forecast accuracy by showing forecast error as a percentage
↳ Calculation: Sum of (Forecast error for time period / Actual sales for that period) / Total number of forecast errors x 100
# 2. WMAPE (Weighted Mean Absolute Percentage Error)
↳ Improvement over MAPE by weighting it based on actual sales volumes
↳ Calculation: Sum of (Actual sales for a time period – Forecast sales for same period) / Actual sales for same period
# 3. Forecast Bias
↳ Assesses whether forecast errors consistently deviate in one direction
↳ Calculation: Sum of observed forecast errors over multiple periods/ Total number of observed periods
# 4. FVA (Forecast Value Added)
↳ Measures whether a step in the forecasting process improves forecast accuracy
↳ Calculation: Forecast Error Baseline – Forecast Error New
# 5. Actual Sales Conversions vs. Sales Assumptions
↳ Compares the sales assumptions with actual conversions
↳ Calculation: (Leads converted into sales / Qualified leads) x 100
Supply Planner
# 6. OTIF (On Time In Full)
↳ Shows how many orders are delivered on time in full
↳ Calculation: (Number of On Time In Full Deliveries / Total number of deliveries) X 100
# 7. Inventory Turnover
↳ Shows how fast or slow inventory is moving. The longer we keep inventory, the higher the chances of losses.
↳ Calculation: Cost of Goods Sold / Average Inventory
# 8. Perfect Order
↳ Meet the 7 R's criteria
↳ Calculation: (Total number of perfect orders/ Total number of orders) X 100
# 9. Customer Order Fulfillment Time
↳ Measures the following cycles: order, source, transform, fulfill, return
↳ Calculation: Sum of Actual Cycle Times For All Orders Delivered / Total number of orders delivered
# 10. Obsolescence Inventory Rate
↳ Measures the obsolete inventory over inventory value.
↳ Calculation: Obsolete Inventory Value/ Total Inventory Value X 100
Any others to add?

author: Adam Smiarowski
captionRaw:
I talk to Supply Chain Directors regularly.
One pattern keeps showing up.
The gap between what they expected from Agentic AI and what actually happened after go-live.
Here's what surprises them most.
1. It works best on repetitive decisions, not strategic ones.
The biggest wins came from high-volume, rule-based calls. Expedite or not. Allocate or hold. Not from strategy.
The system handles the noise. People handle the judgment calls.
2. Deployment takes 6–9 months, not 6 weeks.
Vendors promise fast. Reality is slow.
Change management, data cleanup, process redesign.
None of that fits in a sprint.
3. The biggest win isn't the outcome. It's decision transparency.
Planners stopped asking "why did the system do that?" They started understanding it.
Teams work differently once that shift happens.
4. Clean data isn't optional.
Put an agent on top of messy data and you get wrong answers delivered with confidence.
The AI doesn't know it's wrong. That's the risk.
5. People don't lose their jobs. Their jobs change.
The repetitive part gets automated.
The judgment part gets more visible, and more accountable.
These are patterns, not laws. I could be wrong on some of them.
Which one matches your reality?

author: Samra Munir
captionRaw:
5 ways to write stop scrolling LinkedIn hooks
(That is what I have learned from my own experience writing and testing content on LinkedIn)
1. Start with what your audience already feels
Begin with something your reader already experiences but has not said out loud.
2. Cut every unnecessary warm up line
Remove any phrase that delays the main point or sounds like an introduction.
3. Write like you are interrupting scrolling, not starting a story
Your first line should create a pause, not set up context.
4. Focus on recognition, not creativity
Make the reader feel seen instead of trying to sound clever.
5. Test clarity over effort
Choose the version that feels simplest and easiest to understand instantly.
The hooks that performed best for me were never the most polished.
They were the clearest.
Simple usually wins in the first line.
P.S. A strong hook is not about writing more. It is about removing everything that does not make someone stop.

author: Tom Mills’ post
captionRaw:
How to shift procurement to strategic. Free Guide 🎁
Perception is built on evidence. But the evidence the business sees every day is tactical.
Let's look at the transformation step by step:
1️⃣ Signs the business sees you as tactical
↳ They only involve you AFTER a supplier has been chosen
↳ Stakeholders treat procurement as a box-ticking exercise
↳ You're only measured on cost savings
↳ You spend more time on POs than influencing decisions
↳ Nobody invites you to early planning conversations
↳ Your reports go to Finance, not the boardroom
↳ The business regularly goes around procurement entirely
If 3+ are true, you're seen as purchasing. Not procurement.
2️⃣ The 5 shifts to close the gap
(i) From Price to Value
↳ Stop leading with "we got 10% off"
↳ Start showing total cost of ownership, risk reduction, supplier reliability
(ii) From Reactive to Proactive
↳ Stop waiting to be briefed after decisions are made
↳ Start building relationships that get you upstream
(iii) From Process Enforcer to Business Partner
↳ Stop saying "you need to follow the procurement process"
↳ Start saying "let's figure out how to get you the outcome you need"
(iv) From Tactical KPIs to Strategic Metrics
↳ Stop reporting PO cycle times and savings vs budget
↳ Start reporting supplier risk, value delivered, market benchmarks
(v) From Departmental to Cross-Functional
↳ Stop talking only to direct budget holders
↳ Start building relationships with Finance, Legal, Operations, and the C-suite
3️⃣ Change how you speak
Instead of: "You should have involved us earlier" ❌
Try: "At what point did the supplier conversation start?" ✅
Instead of: "That's not the procurement process" ❌
Try: "Let's see how we can make this work safely" ✅
Instead of: "We need 3 quotes" ❌
Try: "Here's what the market looks like. Let me show you the options" ✅
Instead of: "I can't approve that supplier" ❌
Try: "There are some risks here. Let's talk through them" ✅
Instead of: "We saved £200K this quarter" ❌
Try: "We reduced cost AND improved delivery reliability by 15%" ✅
4️⃣ The perception checklist
↳ Do stakeholders involve you before supplier decisions?
↳ Do you have relationships with senior leaders beyond direct contacts?
↳ Can you articulate procurement's value beyond savings?
↳ Do you bring market intelligence, not just process?
↳ Does the business know what it costs to bypass procurement?
↳ Are your KPIs linked to business strategy?
↳ Does procurement have a voice in supplier innovation?
The gap isn't about capability. It's about visibility, language & how procurement shows up.

Supplier Lead Time Variability
↳ Charges: creates supply chain disruptions, late deliveries, and lost sales that hit both revenue and profitability.

Equalitarian Treatment
↳ Charges: treats all inventory equally, stealing time, focus, and resources from the SKUs that matter most.

SKU Proliferation
↳ Charges: encourages aged and obsolete inventory, creating unnecessary complexity and destroying margins.
↳ Penalty: execute rigorous SKU rationalization.
Siloed Inventory Planning
↳ Charges: generates excess inventory and shortages at the same time, creating operational inefficiencies and cash flow damage.
↳ Penalty: build and run an effective S&OP process.
“Set and Forget” Inventory Parameters
↳ Charges: creates dangerous understock and overstock situations with severe operational and financial consequences.
↳ Penalty: conduct periodic inventory parameter reviews.

author: Marcia D Williams’ post
captionRaw:
Demand and supply planners are NOT the same.
Demand planners do the following:
↳ Predict future demand
↳ Identify anomalies & refine forecast
↳ Impact revenues; top line on income statement/ P&L
Supply planners do the following:
↳ Optimize resources to meet demand
↳ Plan capacity & inventory to align with demand
↳ Impact cost; bottom line on income statement/ P&L
When the 2 roles are in 1, there are higher chances of:
↳ Lost sales
↳ Poor forecast accuracy
↳ Growing obsolete inventory
↳ Greater safety stock & excess inventory
↳ Lower revenues, higher costs, & more cash trapped
*** This post applies to middle and large companies.

author: Matt Barker
captionRaw:
In April, I wrote a LinkedIn post with an 18 word hook. The first line was boring. But the second line broke all the "rules" and the post went nuts. Full breakdown below (you'll wanna save this):
The hook:
"My hottest LinkedIn writing tip of 2026:
Go to ChatGPT and ask it to write you a post."
This post got 69,993 impressions (my average is 14.4k).
But it wasn't the "contrarian opinion" or the "mobile optimisation" or the hook being "8 words or less" that made this work.
It was the SETUP.
Line one looks exactly like every other LinkedIn tip post you've read 1,000 times:
"My hottest writing tip of 2026:"
Boringly familiar and the reader's brain is already deciding to scroll on. But then line two creeps in:
"Go to ChatGPT and ask it to write you a post."
For 0.5 seconds, the reader is confused as hell. "Wait, is Matt seriously telling me to do this?" That confusion is what gets the click.
Here's how to confuse your reader into engaging:
1. Set up an expectation in line one
2. Break it in line two
99% of people obsess over making line one clever but the best move might actually be the opposite:
Make line one boringly familiar, then break it and let the second line do all the work.
That's how you earn the "see more" click.

* Materials
* Information

Lines everywhere.
Crossing. Backtracking. Chaos.

author: Agnieszka Kamila Van der Veen, MBA
captionRaw:
We talk a lot about improvement.
Continuous improvement.
Endless improvement.
Always improve.
But here’s a question we rarely ask:
👉 𝘞𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘦𝘯𝘥 𝘰𝘧 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵?
👉 𝘈𝘯𝘥 𝘥𝘰𝘦𝘴 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘯𝘦𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘥?
Look at the simplest objects around us.
A pen.
A safety pin.
A hairpin.
Decades have passed… and they look almost the same.
Not because no one tried to improve them.
But because they reached a point where:
✔ The function is clear
✔ The design is simple
✔ The value is delivered
✔ The waste is minimal
In other words - they are good enough.
In Lean, we push Kaizen every day.
But Kaizen is not about changing everything.
𝘒𝘢𝘪𝘻𝘦𝘯 𝘐𝘵’𝘴 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘯𝘦𝘦𝘥𝘴 𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵.
Because when we improve blindly, we risk:
* Adding complexity instead of removing it
* Creating variation instead of stability
* Solving problems that don’t exist
💡 The real maturity in operations is not just the ability to improve.
It’s the ability to decide:
👉 This is already optimal for its purpose.
👉 This does not need to change.
So before your next improvement initiative, pause and ask:
* What problem are we solving?
* Is there waste here… or are we creating it?
* Are we improving the system… or just changing it?
Because Lean is not about endless change.
It’s about meaningful improvement.
And sometimes, the best improvement…
is knowing when to stop.

author: Sarah Hurzeler
captionRaw:
Forecasts Don’t Buy Inventory. Plans Do.
And confusing the two quietly drives inventory problems.
Many teams treat forecasting and planning as the same thing.
They solve two very different problems in the Supply Chain.
→ Forecasting
What it is: Demand signal built from history, trends, and market inputs.
→ Planning
What it is: Converting demand expectations into real operational commitments.
The relationship that matters:
Forecasting creates the signal.
Planning turns that signal into action.
Where organizations struggle is in the gap between the two.
When the forecast shifts but the plan doesn’t, the result is predictable:
- Inventory building in the wrong nodes
- Expedites and short production runs
- Working capital creep
- Service levels slipping
Better forecasts help.
But stronger planning processes are what actually protect profitability.
Question for Operators: Where does your organization see more friction today...forecast accuracy or planning response time?

author: Tom Mills’ post
captionRaw:
Strategic Sourcing is as rare as a diet at a Barbecue.
Procurement teams confuse the minimum three bid process as a stategy.
But I’ve seen supplier selection fail time and again as Price is confused with Value.
Depending on the context, three areas to consider:
- Does your Procurement team understand Strategic Sourcing?
- Do you have the time to deliver this?
- Are you adequately resourced?
Let's breakdown Strategic Sourcing into its basic steps:
1️⃣ A product or service is required. Procurement uses specialised sourcing resource to find the best value.
2️⃣ Sourcing team establish a baseline
3️⃣ All applicable vendors identified
4️⃣ Vendors are polled for information (RFI)
5️⃣ Best-fit vendors are selected
6️⃣ Finalists polled thoroughly and submit proposals (RFP)
7️⃣ A vendor is selected
8️⃣ The proposal is further negotiated
9️⃣ Contract signed
🔟 A specialist team monitors contract compliance
Remember the above takes planning and time (a mimimum 12 weeks).
Often businesses can't afford that luxury.
Or Procurement teams feel pressured to deliver something fast.
But the biggest failure?
Most Procurement teams aren't resourced to deliver Strategic Sourcing adequately to truly drive value.
The cost of relying on traditional or three bid benchmarking is too often spend regret and we don't learn the lessons.
I like this quote and it's one to consider when businesses repeat the same spend mistakes year in year out:
“A good failure is when the value of the lesson is greater than the cost of the lesson. A bad failure is when the value of the lesson is much less than the cost of the lesson.” - Alberto Savoia, author of The Right It
Hope that helps!

author: Onesphore RAKOTOMALALA
captionRaw:
✅ FIFO vs FEFO vs LIFO vs NIFO
FIFO is not always the smartest choice.
Know which method actually protects your bottom line.
Each inventory method serves a different purpose in profitability, compliance, and operational efficiency.
Here’s what you need to know:
• FIFO moves oldest stock first → Good for perishables.
• FEFO moves what expires first → Critical for compliance.
• LIFO moves newest stock first → Saves tax, distorts cost.
• NIFO uses replacement cost → Great for pricing in inflation.
The wrong choice costs you: spoilage, overstock, tax penalties, and customer dissatisfaction.
P.S. Your inventory method should align with your product type, market conditions, and financial strategy, not just accounting tradition.

author: Marko Vasovic
captionRaw:
📦 Essential Logistics KPIs (With Formulas) — Track Smarter, Operate Better
Most teams track KPIs… but the real value comes when you understand, connect, and act on them.
Here’s a practical breakdown 👇
---
🚚 On-Time Delivery (OTD)
Measures reliability and customer trust
Formula:
OTD % = (On-Time Deliveries ÷ Total Deliveries) × 100
👉 Target: ≥ 95%
---
🧾 Order Accuracy
Ensures error-free fulfillment
Formula:
Accuracy % = (Correct Orders ÷ Total Orders) × 100
👉 Every mistake = cost + reputation hit
---
📊 Inventory Turnover
Reflects how efficiently inventory is managed
Formula:
Inventory Turnover = COGS ÷ Average Inventory
👉 Low = overstock | High = stockout risk
---
🏬 Warehouse Utilization
Tracks effective use of storage capacity
Formula:
Utilization % = (Used Storage Space ÷ Total Capacity) × 100
👉 Sweet spot: 80–85%
---
📦 Freight Cost per Unit
Controls transportation expenses
Formula:
Cost per Unit = Total Freight Cost ÷ Units Shipped
👉 Track by lane, customer, and product
---
✅ Perfect Order Rate
Measures true service quality (on time + accurate + no damage + correct docs)
Formula:
Perfect Order % = (Orders with No Issues ÷ Total Orders) × 100
---
⏱ Cycle Time
Time from order receipt to final delivery
Formula:
Cycle Time = Delivery Date − Order Receipt Date
👉 Break it down: processing | picking | transit
---
📍 Dock-to-Stock Time
Speed of moving goods from receiving to storage
Formula:
Dock-to-Stock Time = Storage Time − Receiving Time
👉 Slow here = hidden stockouts
---
💡 The Real Insight (Don’t Miss This):
These KPIs are connected:
- Low OTD? → Check Cycle Time + Dock-to-Stock
- High Freight Cost? → Check Utilization + Consolidation
- Low Perfect Order Rate? → Check Accuracy + Warehouse Process
---
📈 Bonus KPIs to Level Up:
- Fill Rate = (Units Shipped ÷ Units Ordered) × 100
- Return Rate = (Returned Units ÷ Units Shipped) × 100
- Cost per Order = Total Logistics Cost ÷ Total Orders
---
🎯 Bottom Line:
Tracking KPIs is easy.
Understanding how they interact is what drives real operational excellence.

→ 9,200 TEU MSC MADELEINE
→ 6,673 TEU EPAMINONDAS
These ships moved out on 18 April with their AIS transponders switched off as they neared the Hormuz and only resumed transmission once they were safely out of the Arabian Sea.
The successful exits of these MSC ships, have brought down the total number of containerships stranded in the Persian Gulf to less than 100 units with a total capacity of 270,000 TEU, compared to a peak of 430,000 TEU.

Update 22 April: UKMTO said that the MSC FRANCESCA and Epaminodes did eventually not make it out and have been directed towards Iranian shores.

author: Julien Lieben
captionRaw:
The anatomy of a Claude Code skill (content edition)
From a team turning 270k followers into $550k/mo.
Skills should be personal, built by you, and built for you, especially with something like content, where having your own voice makes all the difference.
Step 1: What to “skill”
Everything that comes before and after the skill’s output needs to be made by you:
1. Expressing an idea, thinking about what you’d like to say, and touching certain subjects.
2. Output of the skill = AI part = core of the post
3. Refining the output, giving your opinion, adding the instructions & removing patterns you’d never use.
Step 2: Build the content skills
Start by feeding the AI everything you've written:
-All your past posts & engagement data help to see which posts flopped and why & will determine your content pillars.
(if you know people putting out great content, you can also use their posts as a reference for ideas or niches using Taplio)
-Don't write the skill from scratch. Make the AI interview you. "How would you write this?" Your answers become the voice rules.
This gives it your style AND surfaces the patterns that work for your audience.
→ From there, you can build 3 more skills on top: ideation, writing, and repurposing.
Step 3: train it through rejection.
The first 10 posts will ALWAYS be bad. Keep going until they’re not.
→ Give it a topic, ask for 5-10 ideas based on existing posts & personal context
→ Reject the bad ones and approve the good ones and tell it exactly why
→ Ask for the full post, then edit it by hand and repeat what you did for ideation: "this is what I'd write, remember this and turn the patterns into instructions".
Every loop gets it closer to you; the skill compounds as you iterate, so use it every day, to write better & faster.
Hope this helps build your own 🤞

author: Marcia D Williams’ post
captionRaw:
Monday is already too late.
This infographic shows 7 weekly checks every planner should run before Monday morning:
1. Demand vs Supply Gap (Next 4–8 Weeks)
↳ Where demand exceeds supply by SKU, region, or customer
↳ Why: This is where service issues will come from
2. Top Changes Since Last Week
↳ Largest forecast or order changes
↳ Why: Not everything changed. Focus on what did.
3. Inventory Health Snapshot
↳ Excess, shortage risk, slow-moving
↳ Why: Total inventory hides more than it reveals
4. Upcoming Service Risks
↳ SKUs or customers likely to miss service targets
↳ Why: You want to act before the failure, not after
5. Capacity Hotspots
↳ Plants, lines, or suppliers nearing limits
↳ Why: Constraints drive most trade-offs
6. Open Actions from Last Week
↳ What was supposed to be resolved but wasn’t
↳ Why: Unclosed actions compound quickly
7. What Actually Changed That Matters
↳ One simple question: What is different from last week that requires a decision?
↳ Why: Without change, there’s nothing to discuss

author: Angus Craig FCIPS’ post
captionRaw:
Like many people, I’ve been trying to get my head around AI in procurement. A post by Asmaa Gad this week really helped. Her Agentic AI Platforms Map (65 platforms, 10 categories, 2026 edition) brilliantly illustrates how crowded this space has become.
Given the number of platforms and categories, I wanted to step back and understand what they actually do. The discussion that followed provided the answer. AI platforms can broadly be viewed as operating across three layers:
- Orchestration: automating end-to-end procurement workflows (e.g. major Source-to-Pay suites such as Coupa, SAP Ariba, GEP)
- Domain Intelligence: generating insight within specific areas—spend analytics (Sievo, Rosslyn), contract intelligence (Icertis, Ironclad), supplier risk (Resilinc, Prewave)
- Data Access: the foundational layer—connectivity, supplier data, and infrastructure that everything else depends on (Palantir, E2open, One Network)
It’s worth noting that the major S2P platforms are increasingly bundling spend analytics and risk monitoring into their core offerings. So are these truly three distinct categories, or three overlapping capabilities? Perhaps the more useful question isn’t “which platform category do I need?” but “which capability will deliver the greatest improvement in performance?” For most teams, it’s the intelligence layer. The workflows already exist—genuinely understanding what you’re spending, with whom, and at what risk is where AI could close the gap first.

author: Tom Mills’ post
captionRaw:
Most procurement teams want to innovate.
But they're trying to build the roof before the walls are up.
Procurement excellence isn't one big transformation. It's 5 layers, built in a specific order.
Here's what each one looks like based on my experience:
Layer 1: Standardisation
↳ Write clear processes - one way to do the work, consistently
↳ Create supplier templates
↳ Document your category strategies
↳ Define approval thresholds
↳ Train every stakeholder who touches procurement
This is your foundation. Without it, nothing else sticks.
Layer 2: Automation
↳ Implement e-procurement
↳ Connect your systems
↳ Automate PO generation
↳ Minimise manual approvals
↳ Set up spend alerts and approval triggers
Automation without standardisation is just chaos at speed. Do Layer 1 first.
Layer 3: Measurement
↳ Define your category KPIs
↳ Track supplier performance
↳ Build spend dashboards
↳ Run regular reviews
↳ Tie data to decisions - not just reports
If you're not measuring it, you can't improve it.
Layer 4: Continuous Improvement
↳ Gather stakeholder feedback
↳ Spot the process bottlenecks before they become problems
↳ Run small sourcing pilots
↳ Learn from failed tenders
↳ Document what works. Improve every quarter.
The teams that get better aren't more talented. They're more deliberate.
Layer 5: Innovation
↳ Host supplier summits
↳ Encourage bold sourcing approaches
↳ Pilot new supply models
↳ Protect time to explore new ideas
↳ Challenge the status quo - consistently
Innovation without the first 4 layers can be wholly ineffective. With them? It becomes a real competitive advantage.
It's tempting to jump straight to Layer 5.
Then wonder why nothing changes.
Build the layers. In order.
