author: Ronalin L.
captionRaw:
DEMAND PLANNING (NEXT LEVEL)
Most people forecast. Few actually plan.
Everyone knows the basics: What • When • How Much
But real demand planning starts when you ask:
Why is demand changing—and what will it cost if I’m wrong?
1. Not all demand behaves the same
Stable → optimize cost
Seasonal → manage timing
Trend → control scaling risk
Irregular → protect with buffers
Misclassification = wrong inventory, wrong decisions.
2. There is no universal forecasting model
Stop applying one method to all SKUs. Match model to behavior. Segment demand properly. Accept trade-offs (accuracy vs responsiveness)
3. Accuracy is incomplete without direction
MAPE tells you how wrong, Bias tells you where you’re leaning
High bias = overstock or stockouts
Low visibility = unstable decision
4. Forecast = business impact
Every number affects: Inventory investment, Service level, Lost sales or excess stock, this is not reporting, this is financial decision-making.
5. Discipline is what creates results
Before ordering: Validate trend vs noise. Check real demand drivers.
When issues happen:
Overstock → check bias
Stockout → check missed signals
And always: No adjustment without a reason. No decision without impact.
Bottom line, High accuracy alone is not success.
The real goal is balance: Service level • Inventory • Cost
That’s what separates a planner from a decision-maker.

author: Aiman Nadeem
captionRaw:
Inventory formulas don't have to be confusing.
Here's the only cheat sheet you need 👇
1. Reorder Point (ROP)
→When to order. Not before, not after.
→ ROP = (Daily Demand × Lead Time) + Safety Stock
2. Economic Order Quantity (EOQ):
→ How much to order. The sweet spot between ordering too often and holding too much.
→ EOQ = √(2DS/H)
3. Safety Stock (SS):
→ Your insurance policy against Murphy's Law. Demand spike? Supplier ghosted you? SS has your back.
→ Protects against EXTERNAL uncertainty
4. Buffer Stock (BS):
→ Your production's shock absorber. Machine broke? Bottleneck? BS keeps the line moving.
→ Protects against INTERNAL disruptions
The #1 mistake?
Confusing Safety Stock with Buffer Stock.
SS = External (demand/supply chaos)
BS = Internal (production hiccups)
Look at the sawtooth chart:
Stock goes down over time
Hits ROP → you order
Lead time passes → stock arrives
Never. Dip. Below. Safety Stock.
(Unless you enjoy angry customers and 3am phone calls)
Save this. You'll need it.
Tag someone who still calculates EOQ on a napkin 👇

author: Ben Willis’ post
captionRaw:
Deloitte published a piece on the agentic supply chain worth reading if you’re in manufacturing or supply chain.
A few things that stood out:
• Agents support a more continuous planning approach through sensing, decision-making, and response instead of waiting on traditional planning cycles.
• This isn’t one agent doing everything. It’s layered across cross-functional, domain, and task-level agents working together across the flow.
• Dropping agents into existing workflows may miss the mark. Redesigning workflows around what humans and agents each do well provides more benefit.
• Humans still own oversight, judgment, and decision thresholds. Agents operate within those boundaries. Governance is treated as foundational, not something added later.
Deloitte also cited Gartner’s projection that ~50% of supply chain management solutions will include agentic AI by 2030. I can see this happening.
Lately I’ve been using Claude to run some simple agents with anonymized data. Things like checking planning data (lead times, purchase order dates, safety stock, etc.), flagging errors, and suggesting corrections based on defined rules or analysis. I’ve also been using it to run existing Python scripts against historical demand and generate forecast recommendations across different models for comparison and approval.
It’s still early, though the shift is noticeable from a productivity standpoint.

author: Dinesh Krishna
captionRaw:
Forecasting is not guessing — it’s structured decision making.
Choosing the right forecasting method can directly impact:
✔ Inventory levels
✔ Capacity utilization
✔ Customer delivery performance
Here are 4 widely used forecasting techniques every planner should know:
🔹 Naive / Simple Average
Best for stable demand with minimal variation. Quick and easy starting point.
🔹 Simple Moving Average (SMA)
Smooths fluctuations by averaging past ‘n’ periods. Ideal for moderate variability.
🔹 Weighted Moving Average (WMA)
Gives more importance to recent data (e.g., 0.5, 0.3, 0.2). Useful when trends are changing.
🔹 Exponential Smoothing
Applies a smoothing factor (α) to make forecasts more responsive. Best for dynamic and volatile demand.
No single method works for all scenarios.
The real strength lies in:
👉 Understanding demand behavior
👉 Selecting the right model
👉 Continuously improving accuracy using MAPE, Bias & Tracking Signal

↳ AVERAGEIFS: calculate average demand over a rolling period
Data Structuring
↳ TEXT: convert dates into week or month formats
↳ EOMONTH: align data to month-end buckets
↳ WEEKNUM: group demand into weekly views
Forecast Accuracy & Bias
↳ ABS: measure forecast error magnitude
↳ IF / IFS: flag over-forecast vs under-forecast
↳ SUM: calculate total error for accuracy metrics like WMAPE
Data Cleaning & Validation
↳ TRIM: remove extra spaces from datasets
↳ IFERROR: handle broken formulas or missing data
↳ ISNUMBER / ISBLANK: validate inputs before modeling
Scenario & Analysis
↳ PERCENTILE: identify demand variability and outliers
↳ STDEV.P: measure demand volatility; high STDEV means harder to forecast
↳ MAX / MIN: define demand boundaries
Lookups & Data Integration
↳ XLOOKUP: match SKUs across datasets: forecast, actuals, master data
↳ INDEX + MATCH: flexible lookups across large models
↳ FILTER: extract demand by any condition without extra formulas *
Quick Wins (Daily Use)
↳ ROUND: clean forecast outputs
↳ CONCAT / TEXTJOIN: build SKU or customer keys
↳ SORT + UNIQUE: analyze demand by distinct combinations

author: Marcia D Williams’ post
captionRaw:
Replenishment mistakes cost big.
This infographic shows 9 inventory replenishment ways:
# 1 - Just-In-Time (JIT)
↳ When: inventory required for production
↳ Based on: demand, consumption
# 2 - Min-Max
↳ When: inventory reaches the minimum level set; the order is to get to the max level.
↳ Based on: stock level
# 3 - Demand Forecasting
↳ When: inventory required per demand plan
↳ Based on: demand
# 4 - Reorder Point
↳ When: inventory reaches a level that considers average daily sales, lead time, and safety stock
↳ Based on: stock level
# 5 - Periodic Ordering
↳ When: at regular intervals: weekly, monthly, etc
↳ Based on: time period
# 6 - Top-off
↳ When: during downtime, bringing inventory forward to reach capacity levels
↳ Based on: production activity and stock levels
# 7 - Anticipation
↳ When: seasonal inventory, expected demand peak, new system implementation
↳ Based on: expectations about future outlook
# 8 - Opportunistic Buying
↳ When: upcoming price increases, special discounts
↳ Based on: lower price opportunities
# 9 - Consignment inventory
↳ When: supplier-owned inventory is stored at company site until used
↳ Based on: consumption / usage
Any others to add?

author: Alicia Teltz
captionRaw:
⁉️ Are my LinkedIn impressions low because I’m posting too often ⁉️
As an ex-LinkedIn employee, I used to say that there’s no such thing as being punished for posting too much or too little.
Up until LinkedIn made its most recent algorithm change, as further confirmed by TheShieldIndex's data.
→ It proves that your impressions will drop by 65% if you publish content more than 4+ times a week vs. just once every two weeks.
⁉️ ”𝗦𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝗳 𝗜 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲, 𝗜 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹?”
Not necessarily.
Take 3 people with 10K followers each:
𝗣𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗔 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀 3𝘅 𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵
Average reach per post: 16%
Total monthly reach: ~4,800
𝗣𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗕 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀 10𝘅 𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵
Average reach per post: 10%
Total monthly reach: ~10,000
𝗣𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗖 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀 20𝘅 𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵
Average reach per post: 5.55%
Total monthly reach: ~11,100 🚨
Yes, more posts can increase your total reach.
But doubling your output only adds 1,100 impressions.
→ A lot more effort for barely more payoff.
⁉️ “𝗠𝗮𝘆𝗯𝗲 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵-𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘂𝗺𝗲 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀’ 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗿𝘂𝗯𝗯𝗶𝘀𝗵.”
If you’re posting constantly, there’s a good chance quality starts slipping.
But that doesn’t explain the sudden 40% drop for Person C in February.
→ Unless high-frequency creators all decided to publish sh*t content last month.
⁉️ “𝗦𝗼 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻?”
LinkedIn’s new LLM (launched in 2025) has recently been further optimised to:
1. Prioritise persona-relevancy
2. Reduce low-quality content
I spoke about 1. before (see below).
For 2., *my theory* is that LI’s new LLM gives every post sort of a spam-score based on two things:
1️⃣ Content Quality
→ AI signals, promotional intent, harmful content.
2️⃣ Engagement Quality
→ Likely in the first 90 mins or so.
→ AI or Pod engagement, promotional spam, low comment discussion-threads.
If both scores are low, *I assume* LinkedIn throttles your post.
→ Creators who treat LinkedIn like a systemised content machine could be hit the hardest, explaining the sudden drop in their impressions.
⁉️ “𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗺𝗲?”
If your content is GOOD, it will drive genuine engagement, and therefore, posting frequency doesn't matter.
Your posts will still perform.
But if you’re forcing low-quality posts just to stay consistent, I advise posting less frequently and using your freed-up time to:
1. Improve your content.
2. Engage genuinely with others (commenting, connecting, DM’ing).
⚠️ 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗱𝘂𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲.

captionRaw:
📦Safety Stock Vs. Buffer Stock in Inventory Management
Most supply chains don’t fail because of lack of inventory.
They fail because of misunderstanding why that inventory exists.
Safety Stock and Buffer Stock are often used interchangeably,
but they solve very different problems:
🔵Safety Stock is about managing uncertainty you expect:
Demand variability. Forecast errors.
Lead-time fluctuations.
It’s embedded in your system - quietly protecting service levels every day.
🔵Buffer Stock is about absorbing disruptions you don’t control:
Supplier delays. Transport issues.
Operational instability.
It’s tactical - activated when the environment becomes unstable.
➡️ Here’s the real insight:
👉 Safety stock protects performance.
👉 Buffer stock protects continuity.
Strong supply chains don’t just optimize inventory levels…
They align inventory strategy with risk type.
👉 Because not all risks are equal:
✔︎️ Some are statistical → managed through planning models.
✔︎️ Others are structural → managed through resilience strategies.
And treating both the same way?
That’s where cost increases … and service failures begin.
👉 The most mature procurement and supply chain teams don’t ask:
✖️How much inventory should we hold?
👉They ask:
✔️What risk are we protecting against?

author: Marcia D Williams’ post
captionRaw:
We can’t afford inventory misses.
This infographic shows 10 inventory numbers to check daily:
# 1 - On-Hand Inventory
↳ Quantity available in stock
↳ Check: Current Stock Qty from ERP
# 2 - Stockouts
↳ Number of SKUs with zero available stock
↳ Check: Count of SKUs where On-Hand = 0
# 3 - Open Purchase Orders
↳ Purchase orders that are placed but not yet received
↳ Check: Sum of PO lines with delivery date ≥ today and status ≠ received
# 4 - Inbound Deliveries Due Today
↳ Shipments scheduled to arrive today
↳ Check: POs or ASNs with delivery date = today
# 5 - Outbound Orders Due Today
↳ Customer or internal orders scheduled to ship today
↳ Check: Sum of orders with scheduled ship date = today
# 6 - Backorders
↳ Orders or lines not fulfilled due to lack of stock
↳ Check: Ordered Qty – Fulfilled Qty
# 7 - Fast-Moving SKUs Inventory
↳ Current stock levels of high-velocity items that sell or move quickly
↳ Check: On-Hand Quantity of Top SKUs (ranked by recent sales or usage volume over the past X days/weeks)
# 8 - Aging or Expiring Items (Near-Term)
↳ Items close to expiration or aged beyond threshold
↳ Check: Qty or value of items expiring within X days
# 9 - Blocked / On-Hold Inventory
↳ Inventory restricted from use due to quality or system hold
↳ Check: Qty with blocked or quality status in ERP
# 10 - Total Inventory Value
↳ Total monetary value of all inventory on hand
↳ Check: Σ (On-Hand Qty × Unit Cost) per SKU

📊 Demand Forecasting: The Backbone of a Stable Supply Chain
Every stockout…
Every excess inventory pile…
Every production rush…
Usually starts with one thing — forecast accuracy.
Demand forecasting isn’t guessing the future.
It’s reducing uncertainty using data, insight, and structured planning.
🔎 What is Demand Forecasting?
Estimating future customer demand using historical data, market trends, and statistical models to plan production, inventory, and supply chain activities.
⚙️ Two Core Forecasting Approaches
👥 Qualitative (Judgment-Based)
• Expert opinions & market insights
• Useful for new products or volatile markets
📈 Quantitative (Data-Driven)
• Historical data & statistical models
• Best for stable, established demand patterns
✅ Why Accurate Forecasting Matters
• Optimizes inventory levels
• Improves production planning
• Reduces the Bullwhip Effect across the supply chain
⚠️ Common Challenges
• Poor or incomplete data
• Market volatility
• New product launches with limited history
💡 Reality check:
Forecasts will never be perfect — but better forecasting means fewer surprises and smoother operations.

author: Michal Wysocki
captionRaw:
5 things logistics taught me that no university ever could
I’ve spent over 12 years in warehouses, on loading bays, in transport offices, and on factory floors.
Here’s what I know now that no textbook prepared me for:
1. Plans are worthless. Planning is everything.
In logistics, your plan dies the moment the first lorry is late. What matters is how fast you adapt. The best operators I’ve worked with don’t panic — they re-plan in minutes, not hours.
2. People will always be your biggest asset — and your biggest challenge.
You can have the best WMS, the smartest routes, the tightest SOPs. If your team doesn’t buy in, none of it works. I’ve learnt more about leadership on a warehouse floor at 5 AM than I ever did in a classroom.
3. Simplicity wins. Every time.
The most effective solutions I’ve implemented were never the most complex. They were the ones people actually understood and followed. If your process needs a 40-page manual, it’s not a process — it’s a problem.
4. Data without action is just noise.
I’ve seen dashboards that look incredible and change nothing. The real skill isn’t building the report — it’s knowing which number to act on and having the courage to do it.
5. Nobody notices logistics until it goes wrong.
We don’t get standing ovations for on-time deliveries. We get phone calls when something fails. And that’s fine — because the best logistics professionals I know don’t do it for the recognition. They do it because they can’t stand watching things run badly.
If logistics has taught you something the hard way — I’d love to hear it. What’s your biggest lesson from the floor? 👇

author: Marcia D Williams’ post
captionRaw:
Forecast accuracy is NOT bias.
This infographic shows forecast accuracy vs bias.
Definition
↳ Forecast accuracy: measures how close forecasts are to actual demand
↳ Bias: measures whether forecasts are consistently higher or lower than actual demand
Focus
↳ Forecast accuracy: magnitude of errors; how big the gaps are
↳ Bias: direction of errors; systematically over or under
Key Question
↳ Forecast accuracy: “how far off are we?”
↳ Bias: “are we consistently high or low in our forecasts?”
Interpretation
↳ Forecast accuracy: a high accuracy means small deviations overall
↳ Bias: a positive bias indicates over-forecasting; a negative bias suggests under-forecasting
Impact on Supply Chain
↳ Forecast accuracy: low accuracy can lead to excess inventory or stockouts
↳ Bias: persistent bias (positive or negative) inflates costs or drives lost sales
Takeaway for Demand Planners
↳ Forecast accuracy: forecast Accuracy tells you how large your errors are
↳ Bias: forecast Bias tells you which side of actual demand you’re on (consistently over or under)
Calculation
↳ Forecast accuracy: WMAPE=Sum of |Forecast − Actual| / Sum of Actuals × 100%
↳ Bias: Bias% = Sum of (Forecast − Actual) / Sum of Actuals × 100%

author: Christopher Antony Thomas’ post
captionRaw:
Most planners are running their MPS wrong.
They add Forecast + Orders together. That one mistake inflates demand and breaks everything downstream — MRP, procurement, capacity.
The correct logic: MAX(Forecast, Orders). Not both. Never both.
The MPS answers one question: What do we produce, in what quantity, and when?
It converts demand into a time-phased production plan — driving MRP, capacity planning, and procurement.
A negative PAB isn't a calculation error. It's your plan signalling a gap. Find the cause before you adjust the number.

author: Pravesh Dixit
captionRaw:
1. Forecasting:
Every supply chain begins with forecasting. It combines historical data, sales team insights, and economic indicators to predict future demand. This step sets the foundation—if the forecast is inaccurate, every downstream activity is affected.
2. Demand Planning:
Demand planning improves the forecast by adding adjustments and aligning through cross-functional consensus. It ensures that sales, marketing, and operations are all working with a realistic and agreed-upon demand number.
3. Supply Planning:
Supply planning translates demand into production and procurement actions. It considers manufacturing, warehousing, and procurement, all adjusted by capacity constraints. This step answers a key question: Can we produce and deliver what is demanded?
4. S&OP:
Sales & Operations Planning (S&OP) aims to balance demand and supply. Ideally, Demand – Supply = 0, meaning the organization can meet customer needs without overproduction or shortages. This is the strategic alignment phase.
5. S&OE:
Sales & Operations Execution (S&OE) takes S&OP plans and breaks them into weekly, SKU-level actions. Regular meetings ensure quick responses to real-time changes, making execution agile and responsive.
6. Inventory Planning:
Inventory planning combines cycle stock and safety stock within the S&OP framework. The goal is to maintain enough inventory to meet demand while avoiding excess holding costs.
7. Master Production Schedule (MPS):
The MPS converts supply plans into weekly production schedules at SKU level, factoring in lead times. It provides clear instructions for manufacturing teams.
8. Material Planning: Ensuring Raw Material Availability
Material planning ensures that all required inputs are available. It considers current stock, purchase orders, and bill of materials (BOM), adjusted for procurement lead times.
9. Distribution Requirements Planning (DRP):
DRP focuses on distributing finished goods across multiple locations. It adjusts the MPS for different warehouses or regions and includes transportation lead times to ensure timely delivery.
10. Rough Cut Capacity Planning:
This step evaluates whether the supply plan is feasible at a high level, considering major capacity constraints before finalizing production schedules.
11. Capacity Requirements Planning:
Once plans are refined, detailed capacity checks are performed at the weekly level, ensuring that all constraints are addressed before execution.
12. Variance Analysis:
Finally, variance analysis compares actual performance vs. plan. It examines differences in quantity, mix, and price, followed by root cause analysis. This step drives continuous improvement.

author: Marcia D Williams’ post
captionRaw:
Too many metrics ruin supply planners.
This infographic shows 7 metrics that supply planners should actually defend:
# 1 - OTIF (On Time In Full)
↳ Whether customer orders were delivered both on time AND in full.
↳ OTIF = (Orders delivered on time AND in full / Total orders) × 100
↳ Below 95% OTIF is typically a red flag in most industries
↳ Always break OTIF down: is the miss driven by timing, quantity, or both?
# 2 - Fill Rate
↳ The percentage of customer demand fulfilled from available stock. F
↳ Fill Rate = (Units shipped / Units ordered) × 100
↳ Declining fill rate is the first signal of inventory positioning problems
↳ Track fill rate by SKU and product family to pinpoint the root cause
# 3 - On-Time Delivery (OTD)
↳ Whether orders, from suppliers or to customers, arrived when they were supposed to
↳ OTD = (Orders delivered on or before agreed date / Total orders) × 100
↳ Track OTD by supplier; three consecutive misses is a signal to escalate
↳ Use OTD to identify fragile supplier relationships before they become stockouts
# 4 - Weeks of Supply (WOS)
↳ How many weeks your current inventory will last at the current rate of demand
↳ WOS = Current Inventory / Average Weekly Demand
↳ Too high = cash tied up on the shelf
↳ Too low = risk of stockout
↳ Compare WOS against your target range by product category, not just in total
# 5 - Attainment
↳ How much of the production plan was actually executed.
↳ Attainment = (Actual production output / Planned production output) × 100
↳ Low attainment driven by material shortages → escalate to procurement
↳ Low attainment driven by capacity → review production scheduling
# 6 - Plan Adherence
↳ How closely the production or procurement team followed the supply plan.
↳ Plan Adherence = (Planned orders executed as scheduled / Total planned orders) × 100
↳ Poor plan adherence is often a communication problem, not just a planning problem
↳ Set up a weekly check-in with production
# 7 - Capacity Utilization
↳ How much of your available production or warehouse capacity you are actually using
↳ Capacity Utilization = (Actual output / Maximum possible output) × 100
↳ Above 85–90% consistently = time to discuss demand smoothing or additional shifts
↳ Use capacity utilization as an early warning system

he old workflow was dump data into a spreadsheet, fight with formatting for an hour, export something that still looked ugly.

author: Will McTighe
captionRaw:
Your LinkedIn content might get likes and follows.
But when someone needs to hire,
are they going to think of you?
Because in that situation, they pick the person they trust.
Here's the problem...
Writing to educate gets you followers.
Writing to build trust gets you clients.
And you need both.
Here's the system I use:
1/ Pick Your ICP and Make Sure You Understand Them
One problem. One person. That's it.
• Pick a problem you're genuinely excited to solve
• Pick the exact person you want to solve it for
• Complete this: "I help [who] do [what] so they can [outcome]"
• Find people in your ICP and ask them questions
Saywhat started because I was spending too much time writing comments on LinkedIn.
I solved my own problem first, and started talking to other people who had the same one.
2/ Fix Your Profile
Your profile is your landing page.
If people don't instantly understand what you do… they bounce.
• Headline: Who you help + how + proof
• Banner: One clear CTA that matches your content
• Featured: A lead magnet solving one narrow, painful problem
• About: Make it about your reader. How you help them win.
• Photo: HD, no selfies. Solid background. Try InstaHeadshots
3/ Create Your Offer and Build Your Offer Ladder
Start with just one offer.
If you’re selling something, you need to be clear about what it is, and make sure you deliver value to your target audience.
• Free: Lead magnets to capture emails and prove you know your stuff
• Low ticket ($50–$500): Courses that help people get a quick win
• Mid ticket ($1K–$5K): Cohorts or done-with-you programs
• High ticket ($5K+): Done-for-you or 1:1 work
Courses are a lot harder these days because of competition from ChatGPT.
4/ Use the TOFU / MOFU / BOFU Framework
Aim every piece of content at your ICP.
Top of funnel (4x/week):
• Educational carousels and infographics from your real experience
• Hot takes you actually believe
Middle of funnel (2x/week):
• Behind-the-scenes of your process
• Objection-handling posts that tackle the real reasons people don't buy
Bottom of funnel (1x/week):
• Client transformation case studies with real data and screenshots
• Show the result. "Jenny grew revenue by 40% in 4 weeks."
It’s better to have 100 people who trust than 10,000 followers who don't.
Your content has two jobs:
Grow your audience.
And grow your business.

captionRaw:
The S&OP calendar runs the business.
This document shows how to set up the S&OP calendar in 7 steps:
1. Lock Your Executive S&OP Date
↳ Pick one fixed day every month. Block it for the full year.
↳ Example: Last Thursday of the month
2. Work Backwards and Place the Core Meetings
↳ Use this structure:
Exec S&OP → Day 0
Pre-S&OP → Day -5 to -7
Supply Review → Day -8 to -10
Demand Review → Day -11 to -15
3. Add a Hard Data Cut-Off (Non-Negotiable)
↳ Define a date where numbers stop changing.
↳ Example: data freeze → 2 days before Demand Review
4. Create a “Planning Window”
↳ Between each step, block time for actual thinking:
Demand Review → Supply Review → 1–3 days gap
Supply Review → Pre-S&OP → 2–3 days gap
Pre-S&OP to S&OP → 5–7 days gap
5. Protect All 4 Core Meetings.
↳ Don't Move Them.
Demand Review
Supply Review
Pre-S&OP/ Internal Reconciliation Review
Executive S&OP
6. Define Clear Outputs for Each Step
↳ Make this explicit:
Demand Review → Updated forecast + risks + decisions
Supply Review → Feasible plan + constraints + decisions
Pre-S&OP → Annual Operating Plan Gap + decisions + commitments
Executive S&OP → Final signoff of the plan

🔹 Procurement
Driving value through supplier selection, sourcing strategies, cost management, supplier performance, and contract negotiation.
🔹 Production & Manufacturing
Delivering quality products efficiently through production planning, lean management, quality control, capacity planning, and scheduling.
🔹 Logistics & Distribution
Ensuring seamless movement of goods via warehousing, transportation, last-mile delivery, and order fulfillment.
🔹 Foundational Systems
Powering the entire supply chain with IT systems, ERP, data analytics, master data management, visibility tools, and compliance frameworks.

author: Dan Murray
captionRaw:
Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning rod, founded the University of Pennsylvania, negotiated with foreign diplomats, and helped write the Declaration of Independence.
He followed the same daily schedule he created in 1726.
His routine had 6 time blocks: Morning prep (5am-8am) for planning and learning. First work block (8am-12pm). Two-hour lunch for recovery. Second work block (2pm-6pm). Evening routine (6pm-10pm) for reflection. Sleep by 10pm.
Eight hours of work. Two 4-hour blocks that aligned with his natural energy cycles.
Franklin started every morning asking: "What good shall I do this day?" He ended every evening asking: "What good have I done today?"
The schedule's power lies in its principles: dedicated morning preparation, focused work blocks, proper recovery time, evening reflection, and ruthless simplicity.
Franklin followed this structure for decades whilst juggling multiple roles. The consistency compounded. The reflection anchored learning. The hard stop prevented burnout.
300 years later, this works because human biology hasn't changed. Morning clarity. Focused blocks. Recovery periods. Evening reflection.
Plan your morning. Work in focused bursts. Take real breaks. Stop at a fixed time. Reflect daily.
The formula that worked for Benjamin Franklin.

author: Marko Vasovic
captionRaw:
S&OP PROCESS EXPLAINED IN A SIMPLIFIED MANNER
Sales & Operations Planning (S&OP) is not just a meeting. It is a disciplined cross-functional decision-making process that aligns demand, supply, and business strategy.
Here is a simple 5-step view of an effective S&OP cycle:
1️⃣ Data Gathering
The process starts with collecting accurate data from across the organization — historical sales, market intelligence, inventory levels, production capacity, financial targets, and supply constraints. Clean data is the foundation of good planning.
2️⃣ Demand Planning
Sales, marketing, and demand planners collaborate to create a realistic demand forecast. Promotions, seasonality, market trends, and customer insights are incorporated to build a consensus demand plan.
3️⃣ Supply Planning
Operations and supply chain teams evaluate whether the demand plan can be supported. Capacity, materials, suppliers, logistics, and inventory strategies are assessed to build a feasible supply plan.
4️⃣ Pre-S&OP Meeting
Cross-functional teams review gaps between demand and supply. Scenarios are evaluated, trade-offs discussed, and recommendations prepared for leadership.
5️⃣ Executive S&OP Meeting
Senior leadership makes final decisions on priorities, resource allocation, and business trade-offs to align operations with strategic goals.
When executed well, S&OP transforms planning into a competitive advantage.

author: Tomasz Tyras’ post
captionRaw:
The 'Elastic' Supply Chain: Building Scalability for Extreme Seasonality and Flash Sales
The Problem: Businesses face extreme demand volatility from seasonality, promotions, and flash sales. A rigid supply chain, optimized for average demand, fails during peaks (stock-outs, lost sales) and is costly during troughs (excess capacity). The challenge is achieving seamless, cost-effective scalability.
The Expert Insight: An 'Elastic' Supply Chain dynamically expands and contracts capacity in response to demand. It uses flexible manufacturing, agile logistics, on-demand warehousing, and cloud-based tech. The goal is to meet peak demand cost-effectively, minimizing lost sales during surges and excess capacity during lulls. This shifts from static, asset-heavy infrastructure to a dynamic, networked ecosystem of partners and technologies, activated as needed. My experience in optimizing operational agility is crucial here.
Actionable Steps for Building an Elastic Supply Chain:
1. Modular & Flexible Manufacturing: Design production processes and product lines for rapid scaling. Use contract manufacturers to absorb demand peaks without expanding owned facilities.
2. On-Demand Warehousing & Fulfillment: Partner with 3PLs offering flexible warehousing (e.g., pay-per-use, pop-up warehouses) for seasonal peaks or promotions. Leverage micro-fulfillment centers for urban agility.
3. Dynamic Logistics Network: Build a multi-carrier strategy and use freight marketplaces for flexible transport capacity. Implement dynamic routing and scheduling to adapt to real-time demand and optimize delivery density.
4. Cloud-Based & API-First Technology Stack: Ensure core supply chain systems (WMS, TMS, OMS) are cloud-native and API-enabled. This allows rapid integration with new partners, scaling of computing resources, and real-time data exchange.
5. Scenario Planning & Pre-negotiated Agreements: Develop robust plans for demand fluctuations (e.g., 20% surge). Pre-negotiate contracts and SLAs with key partners to secure capacity and pricing for peak periods.
Conclusion: In an unpredictable world, a rigid supply chain is a liability. An 'Elastic' Supply Chain transforms volatility into opportunity, enabling businesses to capture every sale during peaks and optimize costs during troughs. Are you struggling with demand swings, or have you built a supply chain that can breathe?

author: Luuk de Gruijter
captionRaw:
Port of the Week: Oxagon (Port of NEOM) Saudi Arabia 🌍🚢
A port designed for the future. The Port of NEOM is being built as part of Saudi Arabia’s plan to create a new economic hub on the Red Sea. The port expands the existing Duba Port and will serve the industrial city of Oxagon. The idea is a highly automated port, powered by renewable energy, located close to the Suez Canal trade route between Asia and Europe.
Why it could reshape the region:
→ Built from scratch: Few ports get the chance to start from zero. Oxagon can be designed around automation and modern logistics from the beginning.
→ Industry next to the port: Manufacturing, hydrogen production, and logistics are planned around the terminal.
→ Strategic location: right next to one of the busiest shipping routes in the world, and positioned on the Red Sea side, avoiding the Strait of Hormuz.
Why skepticism remains:
→ Cargo still needs to arrive: Ports succeed when trade and industry exist. Much of Oxagon still needs to be built.
→ Strong competition nearby: Ports like Jeddah and King Abdullah Port already dominate regional cargo flows.
→ Megaproject reality: Several NEOM projects have faced delays or scaling down. The famous The Line was originally announced at 170 km, but construction was reportedly paused in 2025 after only a few kilometers of groundwork.
→ Marketing vs reality: Large launch events and celebrity appearances have attracted attention. Critics say the project sometimes looks more like a marketing machine with expensive consultants and expats than a working economic hub.
Time will tell if Oxagon becomes a major Red Sea logistics hub or a very expensive experiment

author: Chris Donnelly
captionRaw:
Building a business on passion < Building a business on profit
Let me explain:
That might sound ill-intentioned.
However, you can be passionate about what you're building...
In fact, I'd argue that you need to be to a degree.
But leading with passion won't ensure your company makes a profit.
You need a model that puts profit as the primary goal and builds from there.
Here’s the framework I use when evaluating a business idea:
Step 1: The First Decision
Is it a business idea or a passion project?
Ask three questions:
1. Who can you help?
2. Who cares?
3. Who can buy?
✅ Profit is your north star
You listen, iterate, and find what people pay for again and again.
🚫 Identity is your north star
It's harder starting from zero, and you risk wasting years.
Step 2: Product Criteria
4 things your product must have:
1. High Margin: No margin = no room to grow
2. Proven Demand: Red oceans beat blue oceans
3. Specific Niche: Focused beats broad every time
4. Content Runway: Can you tell stories about it forever?
Step 3: Niche Down
Get it down to one customer, one product, and one platform.
You can expand later. In the beginning, being niche is your advantage.
Step 4: Idea Generation
7 questions to find a really good idea:
1. What are you really good at?
2. What do you wish someone had built for you?
3. What are your biggest daily frustrations?
4. What could you work on for the next 10 years?
5. What content does your audience already love?
6. What do people ask you for help with?
7. What do you find yourself doing in your spare time?
Step 5: Find Your Angle
Complete your Ikigai:
Love: What excites you?
Good at: Where's your edge?
Paid for: What will people buy?
World needs: What problem exists?
Sweet spot: Where all four overlap
Step 6: Choose Your Model
Pick a business model:
Agency: High margin, founder-dependent early on.
Community: Scales without 1:1 time investment.
Course: One-time build, long-tail revenue.
SaaS: High margin at scale.
Coaching: Hard to scale past your own hours.
Step 7: Scale the Idea
Build a product ecosystem.
8-figure businesses require a product ladder.

author: Eman Abouzeid
captionRaw:
📢How Payment Practices Shape Supplier Relationships?
Most companies think payment terms are a finance decision.
In reality, they are a supply chain decision.
Because suppliers don’t judge you only by the price you negotiate.
They judge you by how reliably you pay.
And that signal travels fast across the supplier market.
👉 A buyer known for paying on time quickly becomes a preferred customer.
👉 A buyer known for late payments quietly becomes a risk.
And when disruption hits — capacity shortages, raw material constraints, or logistics delays.
Suppliers remember exactly who treated them like partners and who treated them like creditors.
➡️ Reliable payment practices do more than settle invoices - They:
• Strengthen supplier trust and long-term relationships.
• Improve access to high-performing suppliers.
• Increase willingness to collaborate and invest in innovation.
• Improve service responsiveness and priority allocation.
• Reduce hidden supply disruption risks.
Late payments do the opposite.
They increase prices, erode trust, reduce collaboration, and often push suppliers to prioritize other customers first.
➡️ In procurement and supply chains, payment behavior sends a powerful signal:
Not about cash.
But about partnership.
Because in competitive supply markets, the companies that pay reliably are often the ones that get served reliably.
Strong supply chains are built on reliable payment practices.
Pay your suppliers on time.
👉 The real question for procurement leaders:
In the next disruption, will your suppliers fight to protect your orders — or quietly prioritize customers who pay them on time?

author: Sergio D'Amico, CSSBB
captionRaw:
Stop guessing where the bottleneck is.
A simple Yamazumi chart shows it in seconds.
Most teams misread a Yamazumi chart.
But this chart makes work balance easy to see.
A Yamazumi chart shows how work spreads across stations.
You compare cycle time with takt time.
You spot where the line loses flow.
***
Why it matters
A clear chart exposes three problems fast:
→ Mura: work spread uneven across stations
→ Muri: one station carries too much work
→ Muda: time spent on non-value work
Now the team sees the issue, not just feels it.
***
How to read the chart
Each part tells a clear story:
→ X-axis: operators or stations
→ Y-axis: cycle time in seconds
→ Stacked blocks: each work task
→ Colors: value work, needed work, waste
→ Takt line: target pace for the line
→ Diagnostic colors: show value work and waste
You can compare stations in seconds.
***
What the bars reveal
Look for five signals:
→ Bars above takt: overloaded stations
→ Tallest bar: the bottleneck
→ Bars below takt: open capacity
→ Large waste blocks: first improvement target
→ Short bars: underloaded stations
Hidden time becomes visible.
Now teams can act.
***
Why teams use it
Teams use Yamazumi charts to:
→ rebalance work between operators
→ cut motion, waiting, and rework
→ support standard work
→ improve line flow
→ guide shop floor kaizen talks
You can build one on a whiteboard.
Yet it drives real improvement.
***
The real value
The chart starts the right conversation.
You see who is overloaded.
You see who has room.
You see where waste hides.
Then the team improves the work together.

author: Marcia D Williams’ post
captionRaw:
Demand planners should NOT track dozens of metrics.
This infographic shows the 7 metrics demand planners should actually defend:
# 1 - Forecast Accuracy (at the right level)
↳ How close the forecast is to actual demand at the level where decisions are made (SKU-family, product family, region)
↳ WMAPE = Σ |Actual − Forecast| / Σ Actual
# 2 - Forecast Bias
↳ Whether the forecast is systematically over- or under-stated over time
↳ Bias = Σ (Actual − Forecast) / Σ Forecast
# 3 - Forecast Value Add (FVA)
↳ Whether the demand planning process improves or degrades the forecast compared to a baseline
↳ FVA = Accuracy_after − Accuracy_before
Positive FVA → planning added value
Negative FVA → planning added noise
# 4 - Demand Volatility (Coefficient of Variation)
↳ How unstable demand is relative to its average
↳ Coefficient of Variation (CoV) = Standard Deviation of Demand / Mean Demand
Higher CoV = more volatile, less predictable demand
# 5 - Consensus Forecast Accuracy
↳ How accurate the final, cross-functional forecast is after Sales, Marketing, and Finance inputs
↳ Consensus Accuracy = |Actual − Consensus Forecast| / Actual
# 6 - Forecast Timeliness / Stability
↳ How much the forecast changes after it should be locked
↳ Forecast Stability = |Forecast_t − Forecast_t−1| / Forecast_t−1
Or
↳ % Changed Volume = Volume changed after freeze / Total forecast volume
# 7 - Forecast Accuracy vs Inventory Outcome
↳ Whether forecast accuracy actually translates into better inventory and service results
↳ Excess Inventory ≈ Over-forecast × Unit Cost
↳ Stockouts ≈ Under-forecast × Demand Shortfall
or
↳ Correlation between Forecast Error and Inventory / Service KPIs

author: Tomasz Tyras’ post
captionRaw:
Intermodal as a Strategic Choice: Moving Beyond the Road for Cost and Carbon
The Problem: Road transport, while flexible, is increasingly unsustainable for long-haul freight due to fossil fuel reliance, congestion, and escalating costs. Companies focused solely on road miss opportunities for cost savings, carbon reduction, and resilience.
The Expert Insight: Intermodal transport (using multiple modes like rail, sea, road with one loading unit) is a strategic imperative. It offers lower carbon emissions, reduced costs for long distances, increased capacity, and improved resilience. This requires a shift from single-mode optimization to multi-modal network design.
Actionable Steps for Intermodal Integration:
1. Network Analysis for Intermodal Suitability: Identify long-haul routes (over 500-700 km) where intermodal options (rail, short-sea) offer competitive times and cost savings. Focus on high-volume, predictable flows.
2. Cost-Benefit & Carbon Footprint Assessment: Compare road-only vs. intermodal, including freight costs, carbon emissions, lead time variability, and capacity. Quantify the "green premium."
3. Partner with Intermodal Specialists: Collaborate with experienced operators for their networks, equipment, and expertise in managing multi-modal movements.
4. Optimize First and Last Mile Connections: Integrate intermodal planning with advanced route optimization for efficient road segments at either end of the journey.
5. Integrate Planning & Visibility: Implement technology for end-to-end visibility across all modes. Integrate data from rail, shipping, and road carriers into a single platform for proactive exception management.
Conclusion: The future of sustainable, cost-effective long-haul logistics is intermodal. By embracing multi-modal transport, companies reduce environmental footprint, enhance efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain. Is your supply chain stuck on the road, or leveraging integrated networks?

author: Marcia D Williams’ post
captionRaw:
Planners breathe inventory.
This infographic shows the 7 inventory parameters that planners CANNOT live without.
# 1 – Safety Stock
↳ Buffer to protect against variability in demand and lead time
↳ Calculation: Z×σd​×√LT​
Where: Z = Z-score (based on desired service level); σd​ = Standard deviation of demand; LT = Lead Time
↳ Review: Monthly or when demand or lead time changes
# 2 – Cycle Stock
↳ Inventory held to meet demand between replenishment cycles
↳ Calculation: Cycle Stock = Order Quantity/2
↳ Review: Every replenishment cycle or quarterly
# 3 – Service Level
↳ Percentage of customer demand that can be met without stockouts
↳ Calculation: Calculated based on target service level factors from normal distribution
↳ Review: Monthly, or when customer requirements change
# 4 – Min-Max
↳ Min level triggers a reorder; Max level prevents overstocking
↳ Calculation: Min Level = Reorder Point; Max Level = Reorder Point + EOQ or another value for the max inventory level
↳ Review: Monthly, or when demand/lead times change
# 5 – Target Weeks of Supply
↳ Defines desired inventory coverage expressed in weeks of demand
↳ Calculation: Policy setting (e.g., A items = 16 weeks, B = 12, C = 6)
↳ Review: Quarterly or when demand patterns or service policies change
# 6 – Reorder Point
↳ Point to order before start using safety stock
↳ Calculation: Average Lead Time X Average Daily Demand + Safety Stock
↳ Review: Monthly or when lead times/demand patterns shift
# 7 – ABC Classification
↳ Segmenting inventory based on importance (A for high value, B for medium, C for low).
↳ Calculation: Based on their percentage contribution to total sales or inventory value
↳ Review: Quarterly

Understanding Key Elements of the Supply Chain: Connecting Operations to Customer Needs
In the complex world of supply chain management, each key function plays a critical role in ensuring products reach customers efficiently. Here's how some core activities align with broader business functions:
🔹 Transportation = Supplier Relationship
Transportation is not just about moving goods; it’s about building strong, reliable relationships with suppliers to ensure timely and cost-effective delivery.
🔹 Warehousing = Product Planning
Warehousing is closely tied to effective product planning. Properly organized storage and management ensure that the right products are available when needed, optimizing the flow from production to distribution.
🔹 Inventory Management = Procurement
Inventory management ensures the right balance of stock, closely tied to procurement strategies that determine what to order and when, ensuring a smooth, uninterrupted supply chain.
🔹 Packing = Demand & Customer Services
Packing isn’t just about protection; it reflects customer demand. Efficient, customer-friendly packaging enhances the delivery experience and supports demand forecasting by aligning with what customers need.
🔹 Distribution = Customer Services
Distribution ensures products reach customers on time. A well-coordinated distribution network not only impacts efficiency but directly affects overall customer satisfaction.
Each part of the supply chain works together to meet the ultimate goal: delivering value to customers.

AI is NOT magic in supply chain planning.
This infographic co-authored with Tarit Mitra shows what AI can & cannot do:
Instant Statistical Forecasting vs Detect Hidden Agendas
↳ AI can: spots trends, seasonality, and outliers across millions of SKUs faster than any manual model
↳ AI cannot: identify sandbagging, inflated targets, or motivations behind the numbers
Real-Time Demand Sensing vs Cross-Functional Conflicts
↳ AI can: ingests POS, web searches, social signals, and weather at scale continuously
↳ AI cannot: won't arbitrate supply vs. revenue trade-offs or sales vs. operations priorities
Scenario Simulation at Speed vs Own the Final Call
↳ AI can: runs thousands of constraint, capacity, and market simulations simultaneously
↳ AI cannot: cross-functional leadership still signs off on the number; AI advises, humans decide
Smart SKU Segmentation vs Build Organizational Trust
↳ AI can: auto-classifies ABC/XYZ, lifecycle stage, and demand volatility to sharpen planning focus
↳ AI cannot: alignment depends on relationships and credibility, not algorithms
Bias & Volatility Detection vs Explain the 'Why'
↳ AI can: surfaces forecast error patterns humans miss and recommends model corrections
↳ AI cannot: tell you why a campaign underperformed or a competitor moved unexpectedly
Consensus Input Automation vs React to Unknown Shocks
↳ AI can: aggregates sales, marketing, and finance data into a single, reconciled forecast view
↳ AI cannot: only responds to patterns in data; black swan events require human judgment
Inventory Optimization vs Drive Stakeholder Commitment
↳ AI can: recommends optimal stock levels by channel or node using live supply chain data
↳ AI cannot: engaging customers, suppliers, and internal teams requires human leadership

author: Jasmin Alić
captionRaw:
Most LinkedIn users are lost right now.
It's why I decided to write this post.
I've trained over 57,000 people how to use LinkedIn for business. This 2-minute guide gives you 26 tips on how to make the most of LinkedIn in 2026:
(Save for later OR Repost now ♻️)
1. Align your topics with your profile. The algo doesn't reward fitness tips from finance experts anymore.
2. Make sure your headline draws people IN first. Your headline is irrelevant once they're already ON your profile. Then, the banner + story should take over.
3. Design a banner that actually has a call to action. 99% of banners I see on LinkedIn lack a CTA.
4. Add a link to your profile. Send visitors to your most desired business offer. Make each visit count.
5. Even if you offer multiple things, pick ONE core offer AND model your profile around it. In 2026, I'll model it around my students: https://linkupbyjasmin.com
6. Add links to posts too. Doing so is fine.
7. Comment more than you post. 4 groups: peers, ideal clients, big influencers, and small creators.
8. Forget posting every day. Stick to 3-5 weekly posts, but make them good. Good content lives longer in the feed now. Frequency won't change that.
9. Add visuals when needed. Faces are most powerful.
10. Stop sharing contextless selfies. (unless you do it all the time, and it's part of your brand)
11. Text posts are making a comeback. Write more.
12. Share your opinions, not just tips and tricks. Information is currency. But your POV is gold.
13. Ask more nuanced questions. Ditch the standard "yes/no" for something more meaningful. People REALLY crave real conversations here.
14. Stop using AI for comments. Just... stop.
15. Write for the first 3 lines of your post. Everything else is irrelevant unless they hit "read more".
16. Share moments. It converts better than just "pro tips". Just last week, I wrote about taking time off, as well as flying people around the world.
17. Most people don't know this but... Optimize your settings here too, especially Visibility. Make sure your public profile is actually "seen".
18. Enable "InMail" in your settings so non-connections can message you. You'll thank me later.
19. Write longer posts from time to time. It works.
20. Post at least 1 video per month. It builds trust.
21. Write daily. Just for practice. Then... Publish your best, and shelve the rest.
22. Stop trying to appease the algo. You will never succeed. This stuff changes on the daily.
23. Talk about your failures more. This stuff connects. Can't all be a highlight reel. But more importantly...
24. Flex more! Not the Lambo. Just overall... Talk about what you've done and ARE doing more. Nobody else will do this for you. So tell us!
25. Support and connect with new creators. Daily.
26. Support small creators too. Daily. ❤️
And voilà! 2026, sorted.

author: Luuk de Gruijter
captionRaw:
German Hapag-Lloyd to acquire Israeli ZIM Integrated Shipping Services
Big move in liner shipping. Hapag-Lloyd, currently the world’s 5th largest container line, together with FIMI Opportunity Funds, plans to acquire ZIM, number 10 globally and Israel’s only container carrier.
If completed, Hapag-Lloyd grows from roughly 7.1% to 9.2% global market share. Total capacity moves to around 3 million TEU.
The structure is interesting. FIMI will take over the parts considered strategically important for Israel. That includes ZIM’s owned vessels and Israeli-flagged ships. It will also assume the obligations linked to the government’s golden share.
Hapag-Lloyd takes the global business. For the Gemini alliance with Maersk, this changes the overall balance between the partners. Based on total fleet capacity, the relative weight of Hapag-Lloyd would move closer to roughly 3/2 versus Maersk, compared to around 2/1 today. That said, only a part of the capacity sits within the Gemini scope, as the cooperation does not cover every trade lane.
Deal value is reported to exceed $3.5 billion. There is no binding agreement yet. Board approvals and regulatory sign-offs are still pending.
Never a dull moment in shipping!

author: Roberto Ferraro
captionRaw:
I recently re-listened to “Indistractable” by Nir Eyal.
Here are ten illustrated ideas from the book 😊
Forethought is the antidote to impulsiveness: don't rely on willpower in the moment. Build systems and plan your actions before temptation hits.
Distraction starts from within: external triggers get all the blame, but most distraction begins with an internal feeling we're trying to escape.
It's also about what you don't do: success isn't just about adding good habits. It's equally about subtracting the bad ones.
All motivation is escape from discomfort: understand that the urge to check your phone is really an urge to escape boredom, anxiety, or uncertainty.
Watch your self-talk: saying "I have no willpower" becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Your identity shapes your actions.
Protect your time like you protect your property: you'd never leave your front door wide open. Why leave your calendar open for anyone to fill?
Your calendar should reflect your values: if health, family, or creativity matter to you, they need a time slot, not just good intentions.
Beware the reciprocity trap: every message you send creates an obligation for a reply. Be intentional about when and how often you ping others.
Use price pacts to raise the stakes: put money, reputation, or a commitment on the line. When distraction has a real cost, focus becomes easier.
Say "I don't" instead of "I can't": "I can't check social media" sounds like deprivation. "I don't check social media during deep work" sounds like identity.
If you haven’t read this book yet, I highly recommend it.
It’s not about avoiding technology, it’s about understanding why we get distracted and building the skills to stay focused on what truly matters.
Which of these ideas resonates most with you?

author: Anisha Jain
captionRaw:
How to prompt Gemini for carousels in 2 mins:
1. Go to YouTube. Find a stupidly viral video.
2. Open Gemini to extract content from the video.
3. Copy paste this prompt:
"Act like an expert Content Strategist and Senior Editor for a leading digital publication. Your goal is to repurpose video content into high-value written pieces that drive engagement.
Analyze the following YouTube video: [YOUTUBE LINK].
Part 1: The Extraction
First, provide a comprehensive breakdown of the video content. Do not just summarize; extract the “meat” of the content using the following structure:
Core Thesis: What is the single most important argument or lesson in one sentence?
Key Data/Facts: List specific numbers, case studies, or hard facts mentioned.
Golden Quotes: Extract 3–5 verbatim quotes that are punchy or profound.
The Framework: If the speaker uses a specific step-by-step process or mental model, outline it clearly.
Part 2: The Angles
Based only on the extraction above, pitch 5 narrow, specific article angles.
Constraint: Avoid generic titles like “Summary of [Video Name].”
Requirement: Each angle must take a specific slice of the content and expand on it.
Format: Provide a catchy headline plus a one-sentence premise for each angle.
Example of a “Narrow Angle”
Bad: How to do Sales.
Good: The “3-Call Close” Technique: Why Most Salespeople Fail in the Follow-up."
4. Copy Gemini's answer.
5. Go to Gamma.app.
6. Click "Create with AI" → "Studio mode."
7. Select "Social" → "10 cards" → "Portrait."
8. Paste Gemini's answer. Select "Minimal text."

Step 1: What approach did you take, and why? Walk me through your reasoning. What was your starting point? What did you consider first?
Step 2: What other approaches did you consider but abandon? Why did you reject them? What was wrong with them? This is where I learn the most - I want to understand the roads not taken.
Step 3: How do the different parts of your work connect to each other? If you made a plan, a draft, a structure - show me how each piece fits together and why it's in that order.
Step 4: What tools, methods, or frameworks did you use? Why those specifically and not others? What would have changed if you picked differently?
Step 5: What tradeoffs did you make? What did you prioritize and what did you sacrifice? Every decision has a cost - show me both sides.
Step 6: What mistakes, dead ends, or wrong turns did we hit? How did we fix them? Don't hide the mess - the mess is where the learning lives.
Step 7: What pitfalls should I watch out for if I do something similar in the future? Give me the "I wish someone told me this earlier" advice.
Step 8: What would an expert notice about this work that a beginner would miss? Show me what separates good thinking from average thinking.
Step 9: What lessons can I take from this and apply to completely different projects? Connect the dots for me.
Make it engaging. Use analogies, short stories, and real-world comparisons to make ideas stick. If a concept is abstract, ground it in something I can picture. I want to finish reading and feel like I actually understand what happened and why - not just see the final result.

author: Daniel Korenblum
captionRaw:
I've spent 2 years figuring out LinkedIn content.
It all comes down to three types of posts:
1. Posts that build visibility
This is the type of content that reaches people who've never heard of you. They're scrolling LinkedIn with zero intention of buying anything. Your job is to say something that makes them stop. Something that resonates with where they are right now and what they're going through.
2. Posts that build authority
Now they know who you are but they're still figuring out who to listen to. This is where you earn trust by teaching them something they can actually use right away. Something they save for later because it's that good. That's when they start seeing you as the person who actually gets it.
3. Posts that build demand
These people are already sold on the problem and sold on you. Now it's about removing every reason not to work with you. This is where you let your results and client wins do the talking. Make them feel like they're leaving money on the table by not reaching out.
One type of content alone won't get you there.
All three work together or they don't work at all.

author: Rahul Mathur
captionRaw:
AI saves me 150+ hours per year for my long form writing - 2026 was the breakthrough year:
I’ve written over 500 long form pieces over the past 3 years - in the pre-AI era, each piece would take 2 hours.
In 2026 - using Notion AI, Wispr Flow, ChatGPT & a few other tools - the average drafting time is down to 30-45 minutes.
Here’s my Writing 3.0 framework ⤵️
Long-form writing can be broken into 5 distinct activities:
(1) Creative spark / idea generation 🔴
- AI plays no role here - ideas come from lived experience which spark your curiosity that leads you down a rabbit hole.
- I’ve tried using AI for idea generation (2025) - but it is fundamentally a recycling machine hence would never meet the creative bar for any good writer.
(2) Hypothesis formulation 🟢
- Here, STT (Wispr Flow or ChatGPT Voice) play a critical role in converting your “verbal diarrhea” into a text based hypothesis that can be used as a research prompt.
- The moment you have the spark - you speak - AI takes due notice!
(3) (iterative) Research & fact finding 🟢
- This is straightforward - esp. with Web Search, Tool calling etc - generative engines are really good at pulling data together.
- Remember: Fact finding ≠ Fact checking; the latter remains a human activity.
(4) 1st draft 🟢
- AI can help you craft a “Writing Style Guide” based on your historic posts.
- For me - Notion AI did a fantastic job based on 500 historic posts.
- Once I have the research & a rough structure, Notion AI comes up with the 1st draft
(5) Final storyline 🔴
- Here, AI plays no role - this is pure human editorial & insight.
- The 30 mins you spend here give the post the storyline, message & arc which readers appreciate
Which brings me to → what has been the big unlock this year?
It is AI-generated 1st drafts
I fed 500+ hand written pieces (from the past 3 years) into Notion AI - with help from ChatGPT, I was able to create a “Style Guide” which emulates my voice, tone, choice of words, structure etc.
The end result is that - the AI first draft is 60%-65% of the way there 🤯
In 2025, AI was saving 30 mins on Research - now it is saving a further 30 mins on Drafting
Writing 3.0 puts a premium on Idea Generation - which means you need to conceptualize proprietary topics OR bring a very different perspective to known topics - which means you need to be a subject matter expert OR go offline to interview these experts 😇
➡️ The ONLY thing you can do as a human writer to stay above the (AI & social) algorithm is to plow back ALL your time savings into Idea Generation - this means visiting new places, going to conferences & building offline relationships to source unique insights.

author: Sahil Bloom
captionRaw:
The most important choice of life…
(a message you need to hear):
Last week, a young mother reached out about her four-year-old son who shows signs of being neurodivergent. She feared he might not thrive in the way all parents hope for.
As a father to a young boy of similar age, it hit me hard. So I shared a story:
A boy asked his father, "What is my life worth?"
The father handed him a stone and said, "Take this to the market. If anyone asks the price, raise two fingers and don't say anything."
At the market, an old woman offered $2 for her garden.
The father sent him to the museum. A man offered $200 for his home.
The father sent him to the precious gem store. The owner offered $20,000 for the rare stone he'd been seeking his entire life.
The lesson: You choose your own worth. You determine your value. You get to place yourself in the right light.
Every attribute has potential for both good and bad. Ambition can lead to suffering if not channeled appropriately. Obsession can create extreme success and extreme loneliness. Sociability may harm focus. Intelligence may spark overthinking.
Your ability to thrive is dynamic, not static. It depends on the light you place yourself in.
In some lights, you'll struggle. Feel undervalued. Underestimated. Ignored.
In other lights, you'll thrive. Feel valued. Supported. Stretched. Believed in.
As individuals, our responsibility is to place ourselves in the right light. As parents, our responsibility is to help our kids find that light for themselves.
You get to choose the light you place yourself in.
This is the most important choice in life.

captionRaw:
I collect great ad copy. Here are the 23 best examples of all time:
1. Fiverr
Principle: The 180 Headline
2. BMW
Principle: The Rule of 3
Use the 3rd line to take an unexpected left turn
3. Hyposwiss
Principle: Punchline First
Write the punchline: "They like us because of our honesty"
Then write the set-up: "We like our clients because of their money"
4. Wall Street Journal
Principle: Trim The Fat
4 words. Pure gold.
"If I had more time, I would have written a shorter letter"
5. Toyota
Principle: The Original
If you can't advertise the latest sexy technology -- call yourself the original version.
6. Wilson's Dog Food
Principle: The Disclaimer
Use the headline to create extreme emotion.
Use the disclaimer to turn it into a smile.
7. Abramson Cancer Centre
Principle: Specific Language
If you're appealing to a specific audience, use their specific language.
8. Freshey's
Principle: Don't Re-Invent The Wheel
So many bread companies are kicking themselves for not thinking of this copy.
9. Plum Holidays
Principle: Sell the YOLO
Everyone is procrastinating on their next holiday.
If you remind them how scarce life is, you create activation energy.

Principle: Reframe expensive items as a selfless gift
11. Hinge
Principle: Call out the elephant in the industry
12. Nike
Principle: 4 words > 4000-word essay
13. Timex
Principle: Create An Enemy
Position the competition as Darth Vader or "The Matrix". Position your product as Luke Skywalker or Neo.
Once someone explains this strategy to you -- you begin to see it everywhere.
14. Rolex
Principle: Sell The Dream... Then The Product
15. The Economist
Principle: Create an Anti-Customer
16. Porsche
Principle: Appeal to their inner childhood dream state.
17. Durex - Thin Condoms
Principle: The Subtle Change
"Your" vs "The".
Gold.
18. Campari
Principle: The Reverse Statistic
If you want to appear more European and less American -- drink Campari.

Principle: Advertising is magic
"Door handles are the handshake of the building; make sure it's a good one"

Principle: Create your own category

21. Porsche 944S2
Principle: Hypnotic Identity Bias
If you don't think this car is exciting, you must be dead. Therefore, if you're not dead, you must think it's exciting.
The most hypnotic ad copy ever.
22. Simons Roof Repair
Principle: Flip The Meme
Take well-known sentences... And insert your product into the conversation
23. Patek Philippe
Principle: Greatness > Objections

THINKING FRAMEWORK (all reasoning stays invisible; only the final deliverable is shown):
PHASE 0 — Instruction Integrity Check

PHASE 1 — Idea Distillation
• Extract the single biggest promise or benefit.

• Identify up to five core emotional triggers (e.g., safety, pride, wealth).

• Build short, declarative sentences (≤ 12 words).

PHASE 5 — Lexical Compression & Readability Gate
• Replace words > 2 syllables unless irreplaceable.

I analyzed 10,000 sales calls and discovered something shocking.
The highest-converting calls had zero pitching.
Just stories.
Here's the systemized approach I use to sell without selling:
1. The Discovery
Stories activate mirror neurons in your brain.
When I tell you about my transformation, you don't just hear it - you experience it.

2. The 4-Part Story Architecture
Every conversion story needs these elements:
Catalyst → (what changed)
Contrast → (before vs after)
Conflict → (what you overcame)
Conquest → (where you are now)
Example: "I was working 80-hour weeks, burned out and barely profitable.
Then I discovered that 97% of success is systems.
This insight changed everything, but I had to systematize every aspect of my business first.
Now I work 4 hours per day while helping 14 million founders achieve freedom."
The gap between before and after = their desired transformation.
3. The Advanced Technique
Start story A, interrupt with story B, finish story B, then complete story A.
This creates hypnotic attention because the brain craves closure.
4. The Psychology Loop
Stories create emotion.
Emotion creates logic.
Logic creates action.
When you master this, you're not selling products - you're selling transformations.
The founder experience is everything.

author: Daniel Bartus’ post
captionRaw:
The Agent Economy is here.
Generational platform shifts don’t just spark new applications, they ignite entirely new economies:
-- Public Cloud unleashed the SaaS Economy
-- The iPhone ushered in the App Economy
-- Social media enabled the Creator Economy
AI brings a similar tectonic shift, and we are now entering the Agent Economy.
We’re increasingly excited to invest in AI Agents for a few reasons, namely:
-- AI agents reinvent SaaS -- incumbent SaaS typically pairs a point-and-click UX, siloed data moat, and seat-based model. AI Agents run counter to all of this DNA.
-- AI agents eat into labor -- labor budgets are 35x larger than software budgets. AI Agents can tap into both budgets.
-- AI agents turn service into software -- markets with low-margin human services historically can now improve efficiency with AI Agents.
When the SaaS economy took off, we enjoyed well over a decade of new born-in-the-cloud application winners. After the iPhone was released, it took over three years for mobile-first unicorns like Uber, Snapchat, and Rovio to emerge. The creator economy did not enter the public lexicon until eight years after Facebook acquired Instagram.
The exact timing for decacorn AI apps is hard to predict, but with early signs of traction, robust foundational investments, and the speed of innovation cycles, we know killer apps are already being built today.

author: Stuti Kathuria
captionRaw:
Clear offers can boost your sales by 50%.
If done right.
Without impacting:
- your profits
- your reputation
Discounts / offers work so well as they:
- Give more value for money spent
- Drive impulse purchases
- Create urgency
While aiding in converting 1st time shoppers.
And selling your slow inventory.
In this post, using Seek's PDP, I've made 5 changes to show how you can leverage offers and 5 other changes to improve conversions.
Changes to do with offers (1,2,6,8,10):
1. Highlight 1st purchase savings in the announcement bar. Show the coupon code for ease of use (can be copied).
2. Show the % savings next to the old price. e.g. 8% OFF or Save 8%.
6. Show savings at a variant level. On bigger sizes or packs. This prompts them to get the higher-priced option.
8. Display offers clearly. These can include 1st order savings or spend X to save Y%. Place this near to the add-to-cart CTA or price.
10. Highlight savings when they buy complementary products. Like completing their routine or look.
Other CRO or UX/UI changes (3,4,5,7,9):
3. Add a short 30s video in the image section. Showing how to use, benefits, ingredients.
4. Use a lifestyle image as the first image instead of a product shot. Creates aspiration for the product and motivates to learn more.
5. Highlight the benefits in bullets. Makes it easier to read and digest.
7. Optimize the area around the add-to-cart CTA. Highlight free shipping and delivery time.
9. Add accordions. It helps shoppers find relevant information quickly.
I also moved the product name, reviews, price above the image. This makes the add-to-cart CTA appear closer. As normally shoppers scroll till the image.
What do you think can be done better?
Found this useful? Let me know in the comments!
P.S. Offers should not make the shopper feel that the product or brand is low in quality. While highlighting offers, make sure you talk about product benefits, positive reviews, third-party credits.
Avoid giving a % OFF of more than 15%. Unless it's an occasional sale like Black Friday.

author: Marcia D Williams’ post
captionRaw:
Because supply chain is all about the customer...
This infographics contains the top 10 🔑 metrics for customer supply chain as follows:
✅ Metric #1 OTIF (On Time In Full)
👉 Meaning: shows how many orders are delivered on time in full
🧮 Calculation: (Number of On Time In Full Deliveries / Total Number of Deliveries) X 100
✅ Metric #2 Net Promoter Score
👉 Meaning: measures customer satisfaction and loyalty
🧮 Calculation: (Number of Promoter Scores/Total Number of Respondents) - (Number of Detractor Scores/Total Number of Respondents)
✅ Metric #3 Perfect Order
👉 Meaning: to be perfect, a customer order needs to meet the 7 R's criteria (APICS)
🧮 Calculation: (Total Number of Perfect Orders/ Total Number of Orders) X 100
✅ Metric #4 Order Fill Rate
👉 Meaning: measures the ability of a company to meet customer orders with available stock, without backorders or delays.
🧮 Calculation: (Number of Orders Fulfilled Immediately/ Total Number of Orders) X 100
✅ Metric #5 Line Fill Rate
👉 Meaning: shows the % of lines the company can fulfill immediately with the on-hand inventory
🧮 Calculation: (Number of Lines Fulfilled Immediately/ Total Number of Order Lines) X 100
✅ Metric #6 SKU Fill Rate
👉 Meaning: shows the % of SKUs the company can fulfill immediately with the stock on hand
🧮 Calculation: (Number of SKUs Fulfilled Immediately/ Total Number of SKUs) X 100
✅ Metric #7 Available To Promise (ATP)
👉 Meaning: shows the quantity of a product that is available and can be promised to customers for delivery on specific dates, without causing backorders or disruptions
🧮 Calculation: Inventory on Hand + Planned Receipts – Sales Orders
✅ Metric #8 Order Accuracy
👉 Meaning: shows the % of orders shipped free of errors
🧮 Calculation: (Error Free Orders/ Total Orders Shipped) X 100
✅ Metric #9 Line Order Accuracy
👉 Meaning: shows the % of line orders shipped free of errors
🧮 Calculation: (Error Free Line Orders/Total Lines Shipped) X 100
✅ Metric #10 Customer Order Fulfillment Time
👉 Meaning: It measures order, source, transform, fulfill and return cycles
🧮 Calculation: Sum of Actual Cycle Times For All Orders Delivered/ Total Number of Orders Delivered

Only 1% of pitch decks secure venture capital—why?

This isn't just about numbers or graphs.

Every slide, every figure, every graph should tell a part of your story.
From understanding the problem to presenting a game-changing solution.
Start with why. End with how.

The list is intended to be dynamic, so don't worry too much about the starting point. It can be as few as 3-5 high-priority items.

He heads straight to the marina to buy the best fishing boat money can buy.
Then, he specs out an expensive, custom, carbon-fiber fishing rod.
And from there, he spends hundreds of hours reading up and watching videos on everything there is know about fishing.
• Weather patterns
• Baiting techniques
• Casting techniques
You name it, he's bought the book on it.
And of course, he's watching the fishing channel every night for hours, learning from the best of the best.
A few months later—after months of diligent preparation—he *finally* feels ready to fish.
So the next day, he heads out on the lake in his new boat with his fancy rod and wealth of fishing "experience" built up over the last few months.
But six hours in, nothing. Not even a nibble.
He fiddled with his tangled rod that was much more difficult to cast than it looked on TV.
Still nothing.
He moved to a spot upstream, just like his favorite guru would suggest.
Still nothing.
So—what happened?
Turns out, the second fisherman had already sucked the lake dry.
On day one, the second fisherman grabbed a shitty rod, sliced up a hot dog, and went out to the lake.
The first day, nothing.
So he moved to a new spot.
Second day, nothing.
So then he moved again.
And on the third day? His first nibble.
From there it was time to iterate.
So every day after, he honed his technique.
He found a baiting technique that worked a bit better.
Or a new lake with a few more fish.
And after three weeks of iteration, he found the winning combination.
Before long, he was hauling in hundreds of fish every day.
To keep up with his daily haul, he hired a small team to help him.
And from there, he opened a restaurant with fat margins to sell his fresh fish.
And after that, he opened a fishing school to teach others his craft.
He did all of this while the first fisherman sat around gathering gear.
Sure, the first fisherman felt productive during those months of preparation, right?
He was "learning" after all, right?
But there was one difference: feedback.
Every day the second fisherman had an idea of something that might work better.
And he went right to the market to validate his assumption.
If it worked, his strategy improved.
And if it failed, he learned something new.
The moral of this story?
Get to action as quickly as possible.
When you find yourself gathering gear, stop.
Grab a shitty rod and start fishing.

author: Krysten Conner
captionRaw:
Stop applying online for your next role.
Do these 3 things instead.
==>FAST RESEARCH:
Find 3-5 people on LinkedIn who work at your target company in the role you want.
I choose a mix of folks who just started & who’ve been there awhile for different perspectives.
Look for people who are active on LinkedIn - commenting/liking/posting every week.
==>THREE QUESTIONS:
Connect with them on LinkedIn & ask for their advice in a SHORT note….
“Would value your advice on XYZ company. I’m thinking of applying & would love to hear about your experience there. Have 3 specific questions for you.”
If they agree, I like to ask things like:
“Why did you choose XYZ company - what’s your story?”
“What’s been the most surprising thing about working there?"
“What's the 1 thing you'd fix about XYZ company if you had a magic wand?”
==>REFERRAL $$:
Most tech companies offer referral bonuses.
There is usually a specific process that has to be followed. (Sometimes, if you apply online before talking to anyone, no one gets a bonus.)
If you’ve had a good conversation with someone- either via email, but ideally via phone, you can low-key ask if they’d like to refer you.
Sounds like:
“I know most companies offer referral bonuses. If you’re open to it, I’d be happy to put you as the referral source. We don’t know each other well so no pressure at all, just wanted to mention it so you could take advantage of any available cash. Really appreciate the time.”
People love to be asked for advice.
And most people want to help.
They’ve been there before.
If you don’t ask, they can’t say yes.

captionRaw:
How I used LinkedIn to apply at 75+ companies in just 3 months. Read on.
LinkedIn search!! I used LinkedIn search to find recruiters and employees at all the companies I wanted to apply at.
How can you also use LinkedIn search?
- Desktop or mobile, you’ll see search icon.
- Just click search icon and select people filter and select company filter also (see pic)
- Type in keywords like recruiter, HR, TA, talent acquisition one after another.
- Send PERSONALIZED connection requests to 15-20 people.
- Start a conversation and let them know your current position and your intent in applying.
- Rinse and repeat process with different companies and multiple keywords.
Around an year ago when I started looking out, I knew my preparation would take 3 months easily.
So instead of pinging recruiters after my preparation, I started connecting with them immediately and told them about my work, portfolio, and my interest in applying for a role at their company after my preparation is done.
And after 3 months when my preparation was done, all I had to do was find a relevant opening from a company careers page and let the recruiter know that I’m ready for interviews.
Also, I connected with even other employees at the company so that they could provide me with a referral in case no recruiter replied me (highly unlikely, but possible)
This is how I managed to get so many interviews in less time.

An AI auto-writing tool that automatically writes your essays and emails for you.
All you have to do is give it a title and a couple of sentences.
3. Temp-mail
Temp-mail gives you a temporary email and inbox to help you sign up for websites and avoid all the spam down the line.
4. Quillbot:
Quillbot is a paraphrasing website that rewrites everything as plagiarism free text.
Super handy if you're in college.
5. Loom
A nifty little tool that lets you record your screen and yourself at the same time, so you can explain things just the way you want to.
6. Otter AI:
Have trouble taking notes in meetings?
Otter records your meetings and automatically transcribes them to text.
7. Pexels:
An awesome website that lets you download high quality stock images for all your work and personal projects.

An insane tool that lets you easily remove the background from your image and add in any background you like.

This website lets you convert files to any format you want for free.
